Students will examine the interconnections between race, ethnicity, and social, political, and cultural frameworks and attitudes that inform community formation and sustaining it.

courses.subject: AAAS
courses.description: Introduction to Black Studies surveys global Black life and culture. Grounded in formative histories uniting Black people across the world - namely the Trans-Atlantic Slave trade, colonialism, contemporary migrations and cultural developments - this course is guided by these questions - How is blackness both a dynamic concept and one that has been constituted across time through various political events, rebellions, forced and voluntary migrations, and cultural forms? How has Black studies evolved in the academy and what are its futures? Through their engagement with various texts, writing, research and presentations, students will explore such questions and more.

courses.description: Prerequisites: Enrollment in the MAc program; or ACCT 30273 and credit for or concurrent enrollment in ACCT 40253; or instructor permission. Business Intelligence & Accounting Analytics combines financial and operational data with mining tools to improve the timeliness and quality of inputs to decision processes. It encompasses both top-down (confirmatory or hypothesis driven) analysis using traditional statistical techniques and bottom-up (exploratory) analysis using database and machine learning techniques to discover regularities, relations, or local structure/patterns that are at first unknown. The topics and related methods discussed include information retrieval and enterprise reporting, classification, predictive modeling, clustering, association rules mining, and social network analysis. The application of these methods are illustrated using modern software tool via examples, homework assignments and group term projects.

courses.description: Much attention has been given to the stress college students are under today. To address this, the course considers what it means to live a 'mindful' life today. What kind(s) of thinking and practice does such a life entail? How would it fit into a busy college student's life? This course will address these questions through both theory and practice. It will range from traditional Buddhist ideas to modern science, from classic liberal arts reflection to contemporary mindfulness exercises. We will consider how practice and reflection influence one another, and how we engage in personal relationships, society, and the natural world. After beginning most classes with a 10-minute meditation, we will discuss the day¿s assignment. We will then generally do another practice and end with a circle of discussion.

courses.subject: AEST
courses.description: Team and Leadership Fundamentals (AEST 20211 in the fall and 2022 in the spring): A survey course designed to provide a basic understanding of both leadership and team building fundamentals. In this course, students will apply learned leadership perspectives while completing team building activities and discussing various leadership topics (i.e., conflict management, motivation, ethical decision-making, etc.). Additionally, students will be introduced to, and practice, basic verbal and written communication skills to develop effective thinking, writing, and speaking proficiencies. Students are taught from the beginning that there are many layers to leadership, including aspects that are not typically associated with these topics. Such aspects include listening, self-assessment/self-reflection, being a good follower, and problem solving efficiently. As a whole, this course provides the student with a knowledge level understanding of the general elements of leader development and effective teamwork. Furthermore, students will continue to discuss the importance of the Air Force Core Values with the use of operational examples and historical Air Force leaders. Leadership Laboratory I000I complements this course by providing cadets with followership experiences.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Food and Culture explores food production, distribution, and consumption for practical and symbolic objectives. The course focuses on the symbolism as an expression of ethics that shape people's individual and collective identities. Toward this end, the course addresses heritage foods and identities at risk due to a change from regional, cottage production to mass production for worldwide distribution. The course also looks at identity in relation to politics and gender. Students learn qualitative research skills, which they apply to a semester-long project in a food-related venue, discovering the ethical moorings of a food micro-culture. Students learn skills for understanding culture through food, applicable to careers and travel in domestic and foreign settings.

Other topics include U.S. Mexico relations, social conflict, resistance movements, religion, and cultural poetics. Student cannot receive credit for ENGL 55713 and ENGL 30713.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: The course introduces students to anthropological theory and methods for application to businesses and organizations¿government, non-government, nonprofit. The course treats a range of topics from organizational culture to product design, marketing, consumer desire, and ethics. The course gives instruction in qualitative research, producing data for informed decision making and creating social and market value.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisite: ANTH 20623 or consent of instructor. Cross-cultural survey of cultural diversity and similarity in the interpretation of health, illness, and healing systems. Examines the interrelationship of culture, society, and health from local and global perspectives. Particular emphasis on the interactions of western and other medical systems.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623 or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisites: ANTH 20623 or 20643, or the professor's permission. This course introduces students to the components of qualitative research, including project design, participant observation, interviews, field notes, and the use of oral, archival, and written history. These techniques contribute to student research projects and ethnographic writing.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623 or 20643, or the professor's permission.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: This course examines topics and perspectives on human-animal relationships (HARE) from multiple disciplines within the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences. We will explore the complex relationships between humans and other animals, past and present, including the socially constructed meanings of animals that shape animal/human interactions and relations within institutions and social, cultural, geographic and interactional contexts. We will consider many types of relationships between human and nonhuman animals, both beneficial and detrimental, as well as the trends that are impacting the future of animal/human relations on the planet.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Analysis and methods in the study of traditional customs and beliefs of Mexican-Americans. Topics may include storytelling and joking, popular religion, ethnomedicine, ethnic identity rituals, and folk art.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisites: C- or better in ANTH 20623 or instructor permission. Explores anthropological and economic perspectives on happiness and human flourishing: the diverse ways in which well-being is conceptualized and experienced in different cultural contexts, the complex relationship between well-being and economic growth, and cross-disciplinary inquiry into the conditions and activities (such as community, ecology, dignity, creativity, generosity, trust, health, and inequality) that engender or impede human flourishing.
courses.prereqText: C- or better in ANTH 20623 or instructor permission.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Development and characteristics of urban societies and the culture of modern cities. Evaluation of theories and methods for understanding the structure, function and change in the social and cultural systems of urban areas.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: The relationship between social science and the study of sports and other play forms; games and play in cross-cultural contexts; American sports and recreation.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: A comparative study of the teaching and learning processes in societies of differing complexity and cultural variability. Empirical data is examined from an anthropological perspective and in the context of theories about culture and perception, world view, rites of passage, culture and personality, and change.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisites: ANTH 20623 or WOST 20003, or consent of the instructor. Explores the anthropological significance of sex and gender as multifaceted and diverse categories of human experience across a broad range of cultures. Studies of sexual orientation, gender identity, reproduction, cultural politics, health, and sociocultural inequalities.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623 or WOST 20003, or consent of the instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Discusses the intersection of food and justice. Investigates injustices generated by the current U.S. food system and by global agribusiness against farm workers in Mexico and the U.S. against residents of underprivileged communities in U.S. cities. Explores possible solutions to these injustices, including fair trade, urban agriculture, food banks, and food policy councils. Students will design an experiential, service learning group project in conjunction with TCU and community partners. (offered as ANTH or SOCI credit)

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisites: ANTH 20623, RELI 10023 or RELI 10043 or consent of the instructor. Anthropological findings in the comparative study of religion and culture across a broad range of societies. Studies of sacred experience, myth, ritual, magic, witchcraft, religious language, gender and religion, healing, and relationships between social and religious change.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623, RELI 10023 or RELI 10043 or consent of the instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: An archaeological survey of the ancient cultures of Mexico and Andean South America, from the first human migrations into the Americas to the Aztec and Inka empires. Anthropological perspectives on developmental sequences and achievements of major indigenous civilizations in both culture areas are discussed and compared.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisite: ANTH 20633 or consent of instructor. An in-depth treatment of basic techniques, methods and concepts of archaeology and a continued update in recent archaeological discoveries around the globe. Research using published site reports and professional journals. Site visitations to excavations in process will be initiated whenever applicable.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20633 or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Origin and distribution of the native populations of selected areas. The historical development and current perspectives of institutions, belief and value systems, and comparative organization of cultural areas. Possible areas to be examined include Native North Americans, peoples of South America, and peoples of Africa.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisites: ANTH 20623 or instructor permission. The course explores globalization's human impacts as understood through the lenses of development, public policy, economics, trade, and migration (among others). The course defines ethics and explores steps toward their realization in three areas in particular: (1) resolutions to social problems, (2) advancement of social justice, and (3) students' career paths.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623 or instructor permission.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Comparative approach to exploring the roles of animals in world and indigenous religions, past and present, including Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, and Native American traditions. Topics include who counts as a religious subject, or person; how focusing on animals can help us better understand religion in general; hunting and farming; animal sacrifice; pets; biotechnology; climate change; conservation; fear & awe; animal theology; and whether other animals themselves might be religious. Discussion-based, coupled with mini-lectures, video screenings, and experiential "meditations.:

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisites: Either one RELI or one ANTH course, or permission of instructor. This course studies the cultures of Syria-Palestine and TransJordan from approximately 1550-332 BCE by identifying and interpreting the relevant archaeological data and anthropological findings. It will explore various aspects of these ancient cultures, including the region's economic, political, environmental, and social relations, as well as its religious expressions and ethnic identities. Additionally, students will consider the significance of archaeological material and anthropological models for reconstructing and interpreting these cultures and for understanding the Hebrew Bible as a cultural and historical document.
courses.prereqText: Either one RELI or one ANTH course, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisite: ANTH 20623 or consent of instructor. Anthropological perspectives on the relationship of Latin American pop culture to Latin American societies. Examines everyday cultural productions, such as dance, music, soccer, television, soap opera, Carnival, and other festivals. Particular attention given to popular culture as a key site where national, racial, gender, sexual, and class identities are constructed, commodified, contested, and globally circulated. Cultural case studies may include: Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, and Cuba.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623 or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Explores the complex interrelationships between people's spiritual beliefs and the environment. Comparative, cross-cultural approach to key features of selected work and indigenous religions, such as cosmologies, sacred lands, agriculture, and animals. Also examines emerging approaches to environment and religion, including ecofeminist spirituality; environmentalism as spiritual practice and civic religion; new green religious movements; and contemporary religious responses to the environmental crisis.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Explores religious beliefs related to the environment and subsistence among Native North American Indian peoples. Investigates topics such as sacred stories and folktales, art and dance, rites of passage, health and healing, and hunting and agricultural rituals. Discusses the changing roles Native American religious beliefs have plays among both native and Euro-American peoples since the time of first contact, from the crafting of pan-tribal native identities to New Age appropriations of sweat lodges and vision quests.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisites: ANTH 20623, or consent of the instructor. An examination of applied anthropology, the use of anthropological perspectives, values, data, theories, methodologies and skills for practical purposes n the real world. Explores the varied domains in which anthropologists practice, the methodologies employed in their work and the ethical and practical problems they face. Surveys potential work sites for anthropologists, examines the skills necessitated by such jobs and explores resources on career preparation and development.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623, or consent of the instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Topics of interest in anthropology, including substantive areas of the discipline.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: An examination of world cultures based on the results of information secured by technologists and archaeologists working in the field. The topical focus may vary each semester.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: An overview of Japanese history and major cultural traditions. Japanese society will be looked at from its origins through the Tokugawa period and onto modern Japan. Religious traditions and cultural perspectives will be highlighted. Additionally, the place of modern Japan in the global community will be examined.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: The course explores French and migrant culture from diverse perspectives. It incorporates readings and films about migration history, economies of labor, politics, identity, citizenship, and civic responsibilities.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisite: ANTH 20623, ANTH 20633 or permission of instructor. This course is offered as either a cultural anthropology or archaeology field school. Phases, methods, and problems of collection and processing in field and laboratory of ethnographic and archaeological data. Issues of public interaction, participant-observation, interviewing, survey, and excavation are addressed as appropriate to the setting.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623, ANTH 20633 or permission of instructor.

courses.description: Senior Honors Research Paper

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: In-depth introduction to human skeletal anatomy including how to identify individual bones, important morphological features on them, and soft tissues that attach to them. Also covers using bones to recover sex, age at death, ancestry, etc., and explores applications in bioarchaeology, forensic anthropology, and other disciplines. Primarily intended for archaeologists and biological anthropologists, but also of interest to students considering careers in forensics, paleontology, or medicine. Weekly laboratory section is required.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisites: ANTH 20623 or consent of instructor. An anthropological examination of the relationship between violence and culture. Ethnographic cases of violence in many different regions, such as Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Western Europe. Topics may include: civil war, ethnic conflict, crime and the structural 'violences' of poverty, racism, gendered violence, famine and disease, and the cultural construction and social consequences of fear.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623 or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisite: Junior standing or permission of instructor. This course explores ongoing processes that link economic systems, multinationals, supranational institutions, armed conflict, poverty, and prosperity in different parts of the world, combining macro and local, native perspectives. Students learn theoretical frameworks and their application to develop ethics that may orient future endeavors in graduate training and professional life.
courses.prereqText: Junior standing or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisite: ANTH 20623 or consent of instructor. An anthropological examination of the relationship between mass media and culture. Particular emphasis on the impact of mass media on the production and consumption of cultural meaning and identities. Inquiry into representations of gender, sexuality, the body, ethnicity, social race, and nationhood in mass media discourses. Case studies of mass media in local spaces and global contexts.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623 or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: For upper-division students who undertake projects in anthropology in regular consultation with the instructor, for one to three semester hours credit.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: An overview of the field, including archaeology, linguistics, ethnology, and physical anthropology. Description and analysis of the profession, its history, theoretical foci, intellectual leaders and current ethical dilemmas. For advanced undergraduates and graduate students with opportunities to pursue individual interests within the field.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.description: Prerequisite: ANTH 20623 or permission of instructor. Principles of descent, kinship terminology and formation of descent groups, including an examination of specific terminological systems in relation to other features of social organization; the adaptive dynamics of family, groups, kinship, and extra-familial associations in simple and complex societies.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: A survey of selected allied health professions and requirements for educational training and career opportunities. The market demands, career earning potential, and associated career opportunities in selected health careers will be selectively focused on in this course. The development and growth of allied health professions within the context of the United States healthcare system will be reviewed

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the healthcare delivery system in the United States in comparison to different systems of countries around the globe. The course explores the drivers of change over time that shape the organization and delivery of healthcare services and opportunities for innovation and improvements in the cost, quality, and access dimensions of healthcare services in these different systems. The course considers the settings in which healthcare services are delivered and the relationships between the different providers of those services and the payers (i.e., insurance companies) of those services. Discussion and learning activities will also focus on the expense of the U.S. healthcare system compared to single-payer and other systems of care and how those expenses translate to outcomes in association with access, equity, and quality of services

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: This course introduces the history, philosophy, and core functions of public health. Students will explore how public health addresses population health disparities using determinants of health. Focus is placed on the key role of data in public health practice, including data collection, analysis, and evidence-based decision-making.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: Prerequisites: MATH 10043. This undergraduate course offers an engaging exploration into the captivating fields of Epidemiology and Biostatistics. Designedfor students pursuing health-related majors, this course demystifies complexities and provides students with a clear roadmap to comprehend health issues and outcomes in populations (Epidemiology) and apply statistical principles in assessing health-related data (Biostatistics). Emphasizing practical application, this course is structured to furnish students with essential knowledge and skills, empowering theirdecision-making in both health sciences practice and research.
courses.prereqText: MATH 10043.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: Prerequisites: Junior Standing; APHS 10003. This course builds on the core principles of interprofessional education (IPE) and interprofessional collaborative practice (ICP) to prepare leaders who drive collaboration, quality, and safety across the continuum of patient care. The course is aligned with the World Health organization¿s framework of IPE in which students of two or more professions learnabout, from, and with each other. Students in the Allied Health fields of Harris Collegetogether will develop the knowledge and skills to be interprofessional leaders within and beyond their respective disciplines.
courses.prereqText: Junior Standing; APHS 10003.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: This course is designed for students to explore emerging, timely, and interdisciplinary issues in health sciences and public health. Topics may include the social and economic determinants of population health; chronic disease prevention; health care technology; population-based research; and translating evidence to policy.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: This course provides a foundation in the theories and frameworks that guide health behavior and the practice of health promotion. Students will examine the behavioral, social, cultural, and structural determinants of health, with an emphasis on processes that influence behavior change across the lifespan. Learners will develop skills in applying social and behavioral theory to design, implement, and evaluate health promotion and disease prevention interventions. By integrating multidisciplinary perspectives, students gain tools to support sustainable individual and community level change and to critically assess the impact of health promotion programs.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: Prerequisites: APHS 10003. This course provides a foundational understanding of health-related communications with a focus on discussions with patients, families and allied health professionals. Designed for students interested in health sciences, the course emphasizes terminology commonly used by health professionals and presents it from the perspective of consumers navigating the healthcare system.
courses.prereqText: APHS 10003.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: This course is an exploration of the traditional healthcare field, including complementary and integrative healthcare treatments from a consumer and healthcare professional perspective. Students will learn to utilize methods of critical analysis to evaluate credible claims made in the marketplace and by government agencies. Consumer protection and rights, marketing, science, public agenda setting, and special interest groups are studied with the objective of developing critical consumers of healthcare.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the health care delivery system in the United States in comparison to different systems of countries around the globe. The healthcare system will be the focus, with an emphasis on the country in which the course is being delivered. This course will explore the drivers of change over time that shape the organization and delivery of healthcare services in different systems. It will explore how services are delivered and the relationships between the different providers and payers (i.e., insurance companies, national health care). The program will have visits to various facilities in the country to allow for an overview of the facility, its services and the funding sources. Social and scientific factors related to health beliefs and practices will also be examined and discussed.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: This course offers an introduction to the structure and core components of the U.S. health system. It begins with an overview of how personal and public health services are organized and their role in shaping population health. The course then examines the system¿s complexities, focusing on the development and functions of health care professionals, institutions, and insurers. It concludes with a discussion of key performance issues within the health system and explores possible future directions in health policy.

courses.subject: APHS
courses.description: Prerequisites: 12 hours in the major need to be completed before enrolling. This course provides students with the opportunity to gain practical, hands-on experience in a professional setting related to the field of health sciences. Through supervised work, reflection, and academic assignments, students will connect their internship experiences to professional goals.

Three hours per week of laboratory, field work, or mentored research activities are required for each semester hour of credit, for up to 3 semester hours credit in any given semester. This course can be repeated for up to 6 credit hours.

courses.subject: ARAB
courses.description: The course will introduce students to the Arabic language and develop the four skills or reading, writing, speaking and listening.

courses.subject: ARAB
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARAB 10153 with a grade of C- or better, or permission of instructor. Continuation of ARAB 10153. This course is the second in a series which develops reading and writing skills in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) with active speaking and listening skills in both formal Arabic and some exposure to the Levantine dialect, one of the major dialects of the Arabic language. In addition to increased vocabulary repertoire, students are expected to obtain a substantial amount of vocabulary and begin to deal with idiomatic language and more advanced syntax. Authentic materials from the Arabic media will be used in addition to text-related video and audio materials. The course also introduces students to aspects of Arabic culture and everyday life in the Middle East.
courses.prereqText: ARAB 10153 with a grade of C- or better, or permission of instructor. Continuation of ARAB 10153.

courses.subject: ARAB
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARAB 10163 with a grade of C- or better, or permission of instructor. This course is the third in a series, comprising both Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and an exposure to the Levantine colloquial. Students will continue development of skills in conversation, listening comprehension, and culturally relevant activities around a serialized audio-visually enhanced story, set in an Arab environment. A greater emphasis will be placed on grammatical structures including reading and writing functional narratives.
courses.prereqText: ARAB 10163 with a grade of C- or better, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARAB
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARAB 20053 with a grade of C- or better, or permission of instructor. This course is the fourth in a series, build on language skills developed in Arabic I-III. It aims to advance students' reading, writing, listening and comprehension skills, enabling them to read and analyze a wider range of texts, including news articles and longer narrations. Students are expected to acquire extensive knowledge in grammar, syntax and vocabulary, with a stress on cultivating speaking skills. They will become more familiar with the Levantine colloquial and gain knowledge of the culturally diverse Arabic-speaking world.
courses.prereqText: ARAB 20053 with a grade of C- or better, or permission of instructor.

There are several required field trips scheduled during class time.

Students study the internal and external factors that relate to one¿s own ability to design, create, and innovate as well as factors that impact a group's ability to act creatively, to innovate, and to produce practical and appealing designs. Students learn and apply principles of design thinking and other creative processes to identify problems, generate multiple solutions, and execute innovative ideas. The class will consist of research and self-reflection in combination with experiential classroom activities including affective, skill-building, and awareness-building exercises. Among the cultures discussed are the Inka, Aztec, Maya, Hopi, Lakota, and Tlingit. All major media are covered.

courses.subject: ARHI
courses.description: This course offers a broad overview of the art of Mexico beginning with the joining of Aztec and Spanish traditions in the colonial period, through the independence and revolutionary periods, and continuing until the present-day.

courses.subject: ARHI
courses.description: Survey of European art during the 17th and 18th centuries with emphasis on major stylistic and thematic developments in painting, sculpture and architecture. Artists studied include Caravaggio, Poussin, Bernini, Rubens, Rembrandt, Velasquez, Vermeer and Watteau.

courses.subject: ARHI
courses.description: Survey of American art from its colonial beginnings to the present day. Emphasis is placed on analyzing works of art critically and examining them in light of their historical and social contexts.

courses.subject: ARHI

courses.description: Occasional courses offering broad surveys of topics, such as the history of landscape painting, portraiture, and public sculpture. Courses may relate to and take advantage of special museum exhibitions.

courses.subject: ARLD
courses.description: Prerequisites: A grade of 'C' or better in DSGN 10133 Color and Light Theory. A series of lectures and laboratory experiments through which students will develop both technical and aesthetic understanding of architectural lighting. Special emphasis on the color metrics, luminaire typologies, photometric analysis, calculations, human centered design, and the lighting design process for both daylight and electrical lighting.
courses.prereqText: A grade of 'C' or better in DSGN 10133 Color and Light Theory. A series of lectures and laboratory experiments through which students will develop both technical and aesthetic understanding of architectural lighting.

courses.subject: ARLD
courses.description: Prerequisites: A grade of 'C' or better in ARLD 20503. This course is focused upon industry-specific digital media used in architectural lighting. Students will learn how to utilize 2D, 3D, and Building Information Modeling (BIM) to create architectural lighting contract documentation, how to generate daylighting and electric lighting calculations, and how to craft renderings through a blending of by hand and digital techniques.
courses.prereqText: A grade of 'C' or better in ARLD 20503.

courses.subject: ARLD
courses.description: Prerequisite: Department major and enrollment in the Honors Program. An examination of a significant issue affecting design, merchandising and/or textiles. The specific topic and presentation format oral, written, graphic, model, garment prototype, computer simulation are determined by the student and faculty directing the study. ARLD 30003 is the first of two courses required for departmental honors. Arrangements for this directed study must be made the semester prior to enrollment in the course.
courses.prereqText: Department major and enrollment in the Honors Program.

courses.subject: ARLD
courses.description: Prerequisite: A grade of 'C' or better in ARLD 20503 and 20513. Students will delve into the interdisciplinary factors of lighting and the human experience. The course will draw from anthropology, psychology, neurobiology and sociology to explore how lighting is perceived and experienced by groups and individuals. Students participate in field studies, writing assignments, research projects, and presentations.
courses.prereqText: A grade of 'C' or better in ARLD 20503 and 20513.

courses.subject: ARLD
courses.description: Prerequisites: A grade of a 'C' or better in ARLD 20513 Digital Media in Lighting. This course will delve into lighting design for residential and hospitality project types. Students will conduct precedent studies to inform their understanding of daylighting and electric lighting design. The lighting design process will be explored through studio style projects including passive design and sustainable lighting strategies.
courses.prereqText: A grade of a 'C' or better in ARLD 20513 Digital Media in Lighting.

courses.subject: ARLE
courses.description: This is the prerequisite introductory course for all ARLE courses. This course introduces many aspects of arts leadership and entrepreneurship, including: mission, vision, and values, nonprofit/public organizational leadership and management, planning and evaluation, financial management, fundraising and development, managing staff and volunteers, audience development, community engagement, programming, marketing and public relations, arts entrepreneurship, and working in the arts sector. The course also introduces students to the nonprofit sector and the current issues and trends affecting arts organizations, such as diversity, multiculturalism, inclusion, and access to the arts.
courses.prereqText: introductory course for all ARLE courses.

courses.subject: ARLE
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARLE 20103. This course covers a number of essential components of leading complex arts organizations, including organizational dynamics and systems, balancing multiple priorities, resources, facilities and functions, developing staff and volunteers, working with unions, and coordinating projects. This course explores effective leadership practices, strategic planning, organizational change, development and learning, human resources management and effective teams. Students develop leadership competencies and skills.
courses.prereqText: ARLE 20103.

courses.subject: ARLE
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARLE 20103. This course covers two important areas of leading a nonprofit arts organization or managing your own artistic career. Financial management includes establishing internal controls, risk management, accounting and financial information systems and professional standards, financial statements, budgets, endowments and restricted funds, earned income, and external reporting through audits and the 990, and tax laws for nonprofits arts organizations. Fundraising and development include trends and motivations of donors to arts organizations, the board's fundraising responsibility, fundraising campaigns, and support systems, planned giving programs, donor relationships, grant writing and management, and fundraising ethics and professional standards.
courses.prereqText: ARLE 20103.

courses.subject: ARLE
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARLE 20103. Arts organizations are increasing their focus on the public dimension of their operations to establish and maintain relevancy. This public service mandate means building and serving multiple audiences and moving towards civic engagement through addressing relevant needs, building partnerships and collaborations and becoming social entrepreneurs. Successful arts organizations understand audience learning, rights, and social needs, and they deliver exemplary customer service,. They utilize interpretive tools, narratives and story, and multiple perspectives as they develop, manage, and evaluate a menu of program offerings and events. The marketing and public relations section of the course covers marketing fundamentals (product, price, promotion, place), consumer behavior, marketing segmentation, branding, effective messaging and communication, and building relationships with media, businesses, government, and community.
courses.prereqText: ARLE 20103.

courses.subject: ARLE
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARLE 20103. What opportunities are available to work in the Creative Economy? What knowledge and skills are required to thrive in a creative economy organization or create and successfully manage your own creative business? This course explores the economic, political, and social environment for the arts and the creative economy. More specifically, the course covers what entrepreneurship means in arts organizations, including the production and presentation of art, utilizing creative thinking and innovation practices to solve many types of problems, and the importance and potential of technology in the creative process. The course also explores entrepreneurship fundamentals and best practices, design thinking and group dynamics approaches, and the steps involved in creating an arts or creative venture.
courses.prereqText: ARLE 20103.

courses.subject: ARLE
courses.description: Prerequisites: This course is the CAPSTONE course for the ARLE minor. Students should have completed the full sequence of their ARLE courses before taking this course. In this capstone course, students apply their cumulative knowledge and skills in arts leadership and entrepreneurship to a real arts organization project on the TCU campus or in a local arts organization, for example, a strategic plan, business plan, showcase, or thesis. Students interested in creative entrepreneurship would create a new venture or apply best practices to revitalizing an existing arts organization, on campus or in the community. Students learn to set goals and objectives, work effectively in teams, design project work to respond to client needs, manage budgets and resources, and meet competing deadlines in a fast-paced environment mirroring real life work as an arts entrepreneur or arts leader. They also utilize best practices in project evaluation as they assess the results of their course project(s) and their team processes.
courses.prereqText: This course is the CAPSTONE course for the ARLE minor.

courses.subject: ARLE
courses.description: Students complete an internship in an arts organization on campus or in the local community, 10-12 hours per week for 15 weeks, totaling 150 hours. Students will also meet monthly with the ARLE program director.

courses.description: General Transfer Credit-FAR

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: This introductory course presents students with a range of studio art experiences that will develop their skills in creating, analyzing, and appreciating art. This class is designed to prepare students from all disciplines university-wide (including non-art majors) to solve problems creatively and to develop critical thinking skills that will act as a lens to understand diverse perspectives. While the specific art media will rotate each semester, this class consistently explores Material, Process, Ideation, and Time as core components in creative practice.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Drawing as a primary art form offers a thorough exploration of the art elements: shape, value, line and texture and the spatial relationship of these art elements. Analytic drawing, perspective drawing as well as expressive approaches are employed. The keeping of a sketchbook is required.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 10103. Creative drawing based on visual experience and imagination. Assigned problems and experiments with a wide range of drawing materials, the use of mark-making tools and inventive exploration of media.
courses.prereqText: ARST 10103.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Study and application of basic principles of creative design.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Emphasis on use of three dimensional media, exploration of materials and introduction to some of the most widely used technical processes relative to contemporary 3-D artists.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 10103, 10113. Basic painting procedures in oil and/or acrylic mediums. Introduction to techniques and material use.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Introduction to basic printmaking processes of screenprinting, relief, and intaglio (etching). Emphasis on creative use of materials and techniques.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Introduction to materials, methods and firing techniques. Wheel thrown and hand-built ceramics.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 10133. Basic introduction to concept and creation of sculpture with emphasis on bronze casting, welded steel, ceramics and wood.
courses.prereqText: ARST 10133.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: An introduction to the concepts, tools and techniques of new media. Students will explore several forms of time-based media while studying related historical and contemporary artists.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Basic introduction to equipment, materials and processes of photography. Emphasis on creative use of materials and visual imagination.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Maximum 3 hours per semester. Directed individual problems to strengthen fundamental knowledge and skills required for advanced studio courses. 1-6 hours.

courses.description: Studies in design research and design history.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 21103 (20100) or permission of instructor. Continuation of ARST 21103 (20100). (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.
courses.prereqText: ARST 21103 (20100) or permission of instructor. Continuation of ARST 21103 (20100). (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: Drawing I (ARST 10103) and Drawing II (ARST 10113). Advanced Drawing expands on Drawing I and II, emphasizing drawing as an independent and experimental art form. Students will pursue projects that integrate technical skills with individual vision and contemporary issues. A wide range of media, including traditional, digital, and cross-disciplinary approaches, may be employed, while students are encouraged to develop sustained investigations into personal themes.
courses.prereqText: Drawing I (ARST 10103) and Drawing II (ARST 10113).

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 20143. Advanced problems in painting with emphasis on individual direction. More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21hours.
courses.prereqText: ARST 20143.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: Any 20000 level Art or Art History course or permission of instructor. Examination of the historical development of Artist Books. It will include hands-on application of visual/verbal statements and present a mixed media alternative for artists from concept through execution. More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.
courses.prereqText: Any 20000 level Art or Art History course or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 20163 or 20173 or 20183, or permission of instructor. Advanced printmaking techniques employed in multiple printmaking processes (relief, intaglio, silkscreen, lithography, and digital) as well as exploration of contemporary trends within the print media field. Individual development of expression is emphasized through independent projects. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.)
courses.prereqText: ARST 20163 or 20173 or 20183, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 20213 or permission of instructor. Advanced ceramic technique; clay bodies, glazes, kiln operation, raku. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.)
courses.prereqText: ARST 20213 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 20213 and/or permission of instructor. Use of ceramic materials on a greater scale as sculptural media. Problems of handling, glazing, firing; scale as sculptural media. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.
courses.prereqText: ARST 20213 and/or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: This course gives students the opportunity to better understand animals and our relationships with them by producing hands-on animal imagery using a variety of media and artistic techniques, including drawing, ceramics, and sculpture.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 10133 and 20243. Sculptural concepts, technical processes and translation of ideas into three dimensional situations. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.)

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Why do many people love butterflies, but fear bats? In 'into the Small' we will explore questions like these using multiple senses and cross-cultural perspectives, and then produce artworks in the contexts of galleries and museum exhibits to share what we find out.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 20503 or permission of instructor. An advanced exploration of the concepts, tools and techniques of new media. This course will explore the creation of digital sculptures, virtual worlds, and experimental studies with fabrication technology.
courses.prereqText: ARST 20503 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 20503. An advanced exploration of the concepts, tools and techniques of new media. This course will explore the Arduino microcontroller and its ability to control our physical world. Students will learn how to control motors, read environmental sensors, and utilize fabrication technologies such as laser engraving and 3D printing.
courses.prereqText: ARST 20503.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 20743, or JOUR 30233, or permission of instructor. Color photographic principles, theory, processes and practice. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.)
courses.prereqText: ARST 20743, or JOUR 30233, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 20743 or permission of instructor. Techniques, methods for producing photographs under outdoor and field conditions. Emphasis on history and practice of landscape photography, its role in the history of the American West and its position in contemporary American Art Photography. (More than 3 hours per classes requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.)
courses.prereqText: ARST 20743 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: ARST 20743 or permission of instructor. Portrait photography fundamentals including lighting, equipment, social and psychological aspects of human representation, and business aspects of professional photography.
courses.prereqText: ARST 20743 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 20743. This course will investigate an extensive range of non-silver, alternative, and post print manipulative processes. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated.)
courses.prereqText: ARST 20743.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 20743 and ARST 30710 or permission of instructor. An exploration of the concepts, tools, and techniques of documentary photography. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.)
courses.prereqText: ARST 20743 and ARST 30710 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 20743 or permission of instructor. An exploration of the concepts, tools, and techniques of studio art photography. All photographs for this class will be staged, fabricated and directed. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated with permission of instructor up to 21 hours.)
courses.prereqText: ARST 20743 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 20743 and ARST 30710, or permission of instructor. An introduction to the concepts tools and techniques of interactive multimedia for artists. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated up to 21 hours.)
courses.prereqText: ARST 20743 and ARST 30710, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisite: Junior standing in Art. The seminar will address specific professional issues such as photography of fine art, compiling slide portfolios, resume formats, exhibition preparation, exhibition venues, the role of museums and galleries, financial concerns and graduate school.
courses.prereqText: Junior standing in Art.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: Junior standing in Art or instructor permission and successful completion of ENGL 10803 and 20803. An exploration of major approaches to art criticism and theory with emphasis on developments since 1900.
courses.prereqText: Junior standing in Art or instructor permission and successful completion of ENGL 10803 and 20803. An exploration of major approaches to art criticism and theory with emphasis on developments since 1900.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: This is a hybrid course that combines theory and practice in the study of feminism and visual art making. This course investigates the distinctive ways feminist ideas can be expressed through multiple visual art media. Through readings, class discussions, and hands-on art projects, students will study examples of feminist art, feminist theory and criticism, and art production. Experimentation with visual media is informed by a feminist perspective and critique.

courses.description: Prerequisite: ARGD 30003 or permission of instructor. Projects in design research and design history. Fulfills the requirement for an Upper-Division Design History Elective.
courses.prereqText: ARGD 30003 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: ARST
courses.description: Prerequisites: Junior standing. This is a team-taught course between Environmental Science and Studio Art. In this course students will explore the ecology and behavior of wild animals to provide insights into the types of stimuli they naturally encounter. These insights will then be used to develop and build objects and structures that will engage and enrich the lives of animals at the Fort Worth Zoo. Students will work in teams to study a specific species currently residing at the zoo and create objects and structures that will enhance their lives in captivity. (Crosslisted as ARST 40553)
courses.prereqText: Junior standing.

courses.description: Prerequisites: ARST 20743 or permission of instructor. An explorations of the concepts, tools and techniques of advanced digital photography. (More than 3 hours per class requires permission of instructor. May be repeated with instructor approval up to 21 hours.
courses.prereqText: ARST 20743 or permission of instructor.
