courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: A survey of selected allied health professions and requirements for educational training and career opportunities. The market demands, career earning potential, and associated career opportunities in selected health careers will be selectively focused on in this course. The development and growth of allied health professions within the context of the United States healthcare system will be reviewed.

courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the healthcare delivery system in the United States in comparison to different systems of countries around the globe. The course explores the drivers of change over time that shape the organization and delivery of healthcare services and opportunities for innovation and improvements in the cost, quality, and access dimensions of healthcare services in these different systems. The course considers the settings in which healthcare services are delivered and the relationships between the different providers of those services and the payers (i.e., insurance companies) of those services. Discussion and learning activities will also focus on the expense of the U.S. healthcare system compared to single-payer and other systems of care and how those expenses translate to outcomes in association with access, equity, and quality of services

courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: Prerequisites: MATH 10043. This undergraduate course offers an engaging exploration into the captivating fields of Epidemiology and Biostatistics. Designedfor students pursuing health-related majors, this course demystifies complexities and provides students with a clear roadmap to comprehend health issues and outcomes in populations (Epidemiology) and apply statistical principles in assessing health-related data (Biostatistics). Emphasizing practical application, this course is structured to furnish students with essential knowledge and skills, empowering theirdecision-making in both health sciences practice and research.
courses.prereqText: MATH 10043.

courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: Prerequisites: Junior Standing; HCHS 10003. This course builds on the core principles of interprofessional education (IPE) and interprofessional collaborative practice (ICP) to prepare leaders who drive collaboration, quality, and safety across the continuum of patient care. The course is aligned with the World Health organization¿s framework of IPE in which students of two or more professions learn about, from, and with each other. Students in the Allied Health fields of Harris College together will develop the knowledge and skills to be interprofessional leaders within and beyond their respective disciplines.
courses.prereqText: Junior Standing; HCHS 10003.

courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the health care delivery system in the United States in comparison to different systems of countries around the globe. The healthcare system will be the focus, with an emphasis on the country in which the course is being delivered. This course will explore the drivers of change over time that shape the organization and delivery of healthcare services in different systems. It will explore how services are delivered and the relationships between the different providers and payers (i.e., insurance companies, national health care). The program will have visits to various facilities in the country to allow for an overview of the facility, its services and the funding sources. Social and scientific factors related to health beliefs and practices will also be examined and discussed.

courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: This interprofessional course is an introduction to aging and/or an overview of the field of gerontology. Major concepts, theories and principles of gerontology will be introduced. Students will explore ageism, current demographic trends in our society, and old age as a stage of lifespan development, health and healthcare concerns of older persons, issues of work, retirement, housing and economics, family relationships and social support, quality of life, and political issues of an aging society.

courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: This course is an introduction to dementia and those people living with dementia. Major concepts and theories of dementia and person-centered care will be introduced. Students will explore the current demographic trends in society, health and healthcare concerns of people living with dementia, issues of stigma, family relationships and social support, and quality of life. Offered as HCHS 30783 or NURS 30433 credit. Nursing majors will enroll in NURS 30433. All other students will enroll in HCHS 30783.

courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: Study Abroad- Partner Program

courses.subject: HCHS
courses.description: This course is an examination of current topics in the area of aging. Topics vary based on current trends and student and faculty interests. May be repeated for credit for different selected topics.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. For new Honors colloquia not yet proposed as permanent courses. Different course subtitles with different content may be repeated for credit.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: This course examines how corporate misconduct creates significant financial, operational, and reputational risks for businesses and their leaders. Students will analyze the legal frameworks governing white collar crime while focusing on risk management, governance, compliance strategy, and practical decision-making to protect enterprise value and stakeholder trust. Teaching/learning methods will include lectures, class discussions of current events and issues, real-world case studies, media presentations, and guest speakers. This course will be a vehicle to (1) deepen skills in critical thinking, (2) explore fundamental legal concepts and analysis, and (3) promote a "values driven" approach to business.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. In this discussion-centered course, we explore a series of unsettled questions in biology, psychology, medicine, and philosophy: What is disease? Are diseases purely biological conditions or is the very definition of disease shaped by society? What does it mean to be healthy or normal? Are psychiatric disorders real? Are disabilities medical conditions or social ones? No previous background in philosophy, science, or medicine is required.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. In this discussion-centered course, students explore and experience empathy in its individual, interpersonal, and civic modalities by way of readings in literature, psychology, sociology, and philosophy.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. In this discussion-centered course, students employ tools of rhetoric, anthropology, sociology, and history to gain new perspectives on the games we watch and play, exploring the intimate links between sports, politics, religion, business, education, race, and gender.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course explores the use of creativity principles to create innovative solutions to cultural and business problems.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course explores the experiential and social dimensions of the Internet, social media and technology.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course explores the causes of crime and the behavior of criminal organizations from the Civil War to the present, using concepts and readings from journalism, sociology, and literature to explore the social contexts and legends of infamous figures.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course examines pervasive and persistent patterns of racial imagery in mainstream U.S. cinema.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course examines the nature and significance of secular society through the lenses of multiple academic disciplines. Topics include the historical forces that gave rise to secular society and the diverse forms of secularization throughout the world.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course empowers students to engage with activist art as critics, consumers, and creators, to challenge themselves and each other by interacting vigorously with a wide range of art works created with the goal of influencing thought and action.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This colloquium explores the social contexts and impacts of current controversies in policing ranging from police misconduct and racial profiling to community policing and media relations.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This colloquium examines topics in the philosophy of mind and cognitive science, including the mind-body problem, the hard problem of consciousness, the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, artificial intelligence, and conceptual disputes in contemporary cognitive science.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This colloquium provides a humanistic exploration the discovery and cultivation of one's unique talents, passions, and duties, not only in the realm of paid employment but in all parts of life.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course examines, using the board game Go as a focal point and an exemplar, various aspects of East Asian cultures. The relation between Asian culture and Western culture and the boundary between culture and natural science are also explored.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course examines the social, economic and political power that Black music has held in "fine tuning" a culture that has not always accepted the individuals who created it.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course explores the philanthropic sector and challenges students to work as a philanthropic foundation that gives funds to local non-profit organizations and as such must investigate, assess, and debate the relative merits of alternative funding targets.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course offers an interdisciplinary exploration of several Western and Eastern conceptions of mind, consciousness, and self through philosophical discussion as well as experiential exercise and exploration.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students use historical research methods and concepts from media studies to examine the meaning of journalistic truth, the role of moral courage in pursuit of journalistic truth, and role of journalism as a bulwark of freedom and human rights.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Using research from psychology, evolutionary biology, nutrition, and neuroscience, students explore what research says about how we can be healthier, happier, and better connected to others.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students use the frameworks of design thinking and systems thinking to develop innovative, impactful solutions to complex social problems.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Through exploration of religious, political, historical, and fictional texts, students examine and evaluate contending responses to the enduring question of what it means to be a good citizen.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Through readings, film, discussion, and writing, students explore critical questions about gender and sexuality in society.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students analyze the pervasive role of Islam in the cultural and political life of the Muslim World via exploration of topics such as Islam and terrorism, Islam and human rights, Islam and the Arab Spring, and the prospects for relations between the Muslim World and the West in an age of globalization and interdependence.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students examine issues of democracy, dissent, and debate in 21st century workplaces, exploring the nature, value, and scope of these ideals in a postmodern, corporatized society.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students examine the history and culture of Texas, drawing on popular song, literature and film as well as social science to hear the voices of many prominent Texans, particularly those of diverse and under-represented communities.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students examine the impact of the Walt Disney Company (including but not limited to its movies, merchandise, theme parks, and television programming) on a range of cultural, economic, and societal issues.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students explore the enduring fascination with Mary Shelley¿s Frankenstein, analyzing the contexts and ideas that influenced Shelley herself and the diverse legacies of Frankenstein in contemporary literature and film.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students trace political and social movements in the United States from the 1920s to the present through the lens of musical theater, exploring how issues of class, gender/sexuality, race, and national identity play out on the stage and screen.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students explore what it means to live a mindful life in the 21st century and the kinds of thinking and practices that such a life entails.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students examine the nature, value, and challenges of game-based learning in a variety of fields, exploring the work/play divide, gamification, and participatory culture.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students gain insight into a range of social and personal issues, from the climate change debate to medical advice from physicians, by examining key texts and ideas from the history of science.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students draw upon the medical humanities, memoir, and science fiction to explore what caregiving and care ethics look like in a time when our own planet is facing a health crisis.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students examine the future of American leadership in a rapidly changing global context.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students critically and comparatively explore the depiction of monstrous parents (particularly mothers) in film, literature, and medical history.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Through comparative examination of English-language newspapers and news sites in over 100 countries, students identify cultural differences and similarities across nations and explore the tensions between globalization and cultural identity.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Through first-hand exposure to speeches and texts by former presidents and prime ministers across the Americas, students examine elements of executive leadership and advantages and disadvantages of presidential and prime ministerial systems.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Using learning materials and perspectives from multiple disciplines and cultural contexts, students examine the internal and external resiliencies that allow humans to endure and thrive in the most difficult of circumstances.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students study the narratives of pregnant people, using the methods of Narrative Medicine to understand how the power of story and how legal, political, medical, and cultural circumstances shape personal experiences of pregnancy and decisions around pregnancy care.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students reflect upon cultural standards and norms embedded in contemporary novels and films, by means of which certain characters are rendered despicable, marginal, or lesser.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students in this site-based course learn to read the spaces around them as vibrant, evolving, historical texts.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. Students examine the worldly nature and significance of games and gaming communities, in part by learning to play and reflect upon well-known video games.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College.. Students examine popular dystopic depictions of the future (via games, films, and literature), seeking to understand how technology changes our perceptions of reality and humanity.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College..

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors. Students examine hero myths across multiple cultural contexts to explore how they reflect and/or critique their cultural contexts while simultaneously shaping readers¿ cultural identities.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors. Students understand the nature and significance of sustainability, climate change, and the tradeoffs facing us, individually and globally, in the 21st century.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors. Students explore theories and forms of capitalism and socialism, past and present, seeking to understand their promises and failures to generate freedom, fairness, and prosperity for all.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors. Students seek to understand the present age by asking what is new about it compared to the era of modernity (1450-1918).
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors. Students study the goals and practices of Universities Studying Slavery, reflect on their own campus culture through this comparative lens, and consider additional ways to create a more inclusive and equitable campus community.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College and declared pursuit of University Honors.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College. This course explores the cultural phenomena of witches, witchcraft and witch hunts with a special focus on the 1692 Salem witch hysteria. The course includes examining primary and secondary sources, case studies, popular literature and movies to gain a greater understanding of the role that that witches and witchcraft play in contemporary society.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Acceptance into the Honors College.This course helps students develop a deeper understanding of the ideals, principles, and beliefs that guide their behavior and how they experience the world around them. Students will grapple with questions around sites of tragedy, monuments, and gentrification of communities. Through an interdisciplinary lens, students interrogate how place and space form our understanding of the world and ourselves.
courses.prereqText: Acceptance into the Honors College.This course helps students develop a deeper understanding of the ideals, principles, and beliefs that guide their behavior and how they experience the world around them.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisite: Must be in the Honors College. Great ideas die all the time. This course is interested in what circumstances elevate certain ideas while sweeping others to the dustbins of history. Examining the rhetorical strategies around some of the world's "biggest ideas," we will debate and evaluate which tactics proved effective and how we can sharpen our persuasive skills to become better advocates for ourselves and our ideas. This class will culminate in a TED Talk-style presentation where students will discover, develop, and deliver their own keynotes to gain a better understanding of what it takes to achieve the perfect pitch.
courses.prereqText: Must be in the Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOL
courses.description: Prerequisites: Must be in Honors College. In this course, we will explore the nature of public apologies and the work that they do, while interrogating what actually constitutes an expression of remorse and repair in our hyper-mediated environment. We will explore the modern mediated ritual of apology and forgiveness, asking in particular who gets to apologize, who is asked to forgive, and what the difference is between these two processes. In particular, we will interrogate: WHO gets to apologize? WHO is asked to forgive? WHEN do apologies happen? HOW do apologies work? What¿s the difference between apologies and expressions of remorse? Who has the POWER in the apology dynamic? What role does MEDIA play in communicating and negotiating apologies? Who is asked to `turn the other cheek?¿ What role does RELIGION play in the narrative of forgiveness?
courses.prereqText: Must be in Honors College.

courses.subject: HCOM
courses.description: This class aims to provide you with an overview of the field of health communication and enhance your understanding about it. Specifically, you will learn most studied major topical areas in healthcare and health communication, theories and methods used to guide health communication research and intervention, and design and evaluations of health campaigns. Students may not receive credit for both HCOM 10313 and COMM 30313.

courses.subject: HCOM
courses.description: A beginning look at issues and opportunities in the areas of health, communication and media. This class is designed to help students examine social and media forces of health communication that impact diverse groups. Topics will include health promotion campaigns, media health edutainment, interpersonal health communication and media advocacy and outreach.

courses.subject: HCOM
courses.description: The quality of relational communication is fundamentally tied to human health. This course aims to better understand how interpersonal communication affects people's physiological well-being by studying the health outcomes associated with relational processes like emotional expression, disclosure, affection, and conflict.

courses.subject: HCOM
courses.description: Prerequisites: HCOM 10313 or 20303. Globalization, technological advancement, and new media have been revolutionized and complicated issues in health communication and healthcare. This class is designed to help students examine social and media forces of health communication that impact diverse groups in the 21st century. We will take a close examination of the latest issues and opportunities in the areas of health, communication and media. Topics will include e-health, m-health, telemedicine, health campaigns, culture and diversity in healthcare.

courses.subject: HCOM
courses.description: Prerequisites: HCOM 10313 and 20303. Learn how a health communication campaign is created and executed. Students will utilize their accumulated knowledge from their minor courses to analyze health campaign case studies, then create and execute a health communication campaign as a team.

courses.subject: HCOM
courses.description: Prerequisite: HCOM 10313 or 20303. Specific topics requiring independent or small group research and study in health communication.

courses.subject: HEBR
courses.description: The course aims at building a firm foundation in basic biblical Hebrew with a view toward productive academic engagement with the documents of the Old Testament/Hebrew Bible. We will cover the basics of Hebrew morphology (the way words are put together), syntax (the way phrases and sentences are put together), and vocabulary. These will be strengthened by continual review through memorization, exercises, quizzes, and exams.

courses.subject: HEBR
courses.description: This course will help students to continue building a firm foundation in basic biblical Hebrew with a view toward productive academic engagement with the documents of the Old Testament/Hebrew Bible. This foundation will be laid by absorption of the basics of Hebrew morphology (the way words are put together), syntax (the way phrases and sentences are put together), and vocabulary, and strengthened by continual review through memorization, exercises, quizzes, translation projects, and exams.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Transfer work with TCUCC-HT, HUM credit.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Explores themes and topics in world history from the origins of civilization to 1500.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This is a lower-division, lecture course covering global development from around 1500 CE to the 21st century. It covers the main political, social, and cultural trends in a variety of societies while at the same time stressing the global perspective. Thus, the first goal is learning the specific histories and cultures within a comparative global context. The rise and fall of civilizations, empires, and states will be studied within the conceptual frameworks including modernity, nation states, imperialism, and colonialism. A second goal of the course is to develop the critical and analytical skills of students. In addition to learning historical content, students will also be engaged in the analysis of writing history through discussing a wide range of primary sources including museum objects and archival documents.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course will explore the path of European history from the origins of civilization to 1348. Its principal elements include the early societies of Mesopotamia, Egypt and Israel, the political and cultural contribution of Greece and Rome, the rise of Christianity and Islam, the characteristics of the medieval world, and the Black Death. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: History elective credit in transfer.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course will explore the history of Europe in the early modern period, bracketed by the Black Death and the French Revolution. Principal themes include the artistic achievements of the Renaissance, the expansion of education and literacy, the invention of the printing press, the religious conflicts of the Reformation, the growth of centralized nation-states, the dramatic discoveries of the Scientific Revolution, and the creation of a global framework for the European experience. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines the history of Europe in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and will identify, explore, and define the developments of modern European history. The course will focus on the common heritage and themes that make it possible to speak of 'European' history, while at the same time developing an appreciation for regional and cultural variations. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This is a lower-division lecture course covering major transformations in Africa from the 1800 to the 21st century. Readings are carefully sampled thematically and geographically, introducing students to questions of statecraft, class, gender, ethnicity, violence, environment, and decolonization in precolonial, colonial, and postcolonial African contexts. This course analyzes variegated impact of the Atlantic slave trade, abolition, and the "legitimate" commerce on societies, states, and peoples.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: General Transfer Credit-HT, SSC credit.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Transfer work with UCR/TCUCC credit.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This seminar gives first-year students hands-on experience with primary sources and other historical materials.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: History transfer work with HT/HUM only credit.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Transfer work with TCUCC credit.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Review of evolution of the American nation from the discovery of the New World to the end of the Civil War era, with emphasis on major forces shaping its development. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Review of the emergence of the American nation through the transitional crises of the past hundred years, with emphasis on the roots of movements persisting into the modern period. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Transfer work

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Comprehensive survey of African Americans in the United States from 1619 to 1968 with special emphasis on the internal changes (such as citizenship, work, family, culture, religion, and community) and external challenges (such as slavery, racial segregation, urbanization, industrialization, major wars, and mass migrations) faced by African Americans from the start of the Transatlantic Slave Trade to the culmination of the Civil Rights Movement. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: A thematic survey of the making of the United States from a multicultural perspective. Spanning the precolonial era to the present, the course includes units on Native Americans, African Americans, Asian Americans, European immigrants, and Latinos/as--analyzing the different groups comparatively and in relationship to one another. In addition to history, the course includes elements of Critical Race and Ethnic Studies and explores the intersections between race/ethnicity, class, gender, and sexuality. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: A comprehensive history of Latinas/os in the United States from settlement to present, with an emphasis on the period since 1848. This course covers the cultural, political, and economic contexts of identity and community formation, immigration, and labor and civil rights struggles among various Latina/o communities within the United States.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Transfer work

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course surveys the history of the Middle East from the rise of Islam to the end of the sixteenth century. Students will be introduced to basic aspects of the political, social, and cultural dimensions of Islamic civilization from Spain to Iran as they changed over time. Central themes include the emergence of Sunni and Shi'i identities, the relationship of Muslims and non-Muslims, and the unique material and intellectual contribution of Islamic civilization to world history and other societies. (ME)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Transfer work

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: How has the Middle East changed across the modern period? What are the main political, cultural, and socioeconomic forces¿both local and global¿that shaped this highly diverse region of the world? This course surveys key developments in the history of the modern Middle East and North Africa, including the spread of new political ideologies and cultural trends in the Ottoman and Persian Empires, the emergence of modern nation states, European imperialism, twentieth-century decolonization movements, and twenty-first century socioeconomic and geopolitical shifts and conflicts.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This survey course covers the practice of slavery in the Islamic world from the time of Prophet Muhammad to the 20th century. Students will learn about not only the diverse histories of different Islamic societies from Southeast Asia to North Africa and Americas, they will also study the similarities and differences of slavery as an institution in these societies. The themes covered in the course include concubinage, slave dynasties, elite and military slavery, race and slavery, slave trade, manumission, and abolition of slavery.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This lecture course covers the history of corsairs and pirates in the Mediterranean in the early modern period, i.e. the 16th to early 19th centuries. The main goal of the course is providing a historical context for the 'external war' between the Christendom and Islamic world in the Mediterranean. Through our weekly discussions, students will acquire the analytical skills to problematize the geographic, religious, and ethnic divisions between Europe, Asia, Africa, and America as well as those between Islam and Christianity.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course introduces students to the history of Latin America and the Caribbean through film. From early encounters to more recent social movements, we will use both fictional and documentary cinema to engage with some of the most dramatic and pivotal events in the region¿s past. Designed for students of all majors, the class emphasizes accessibility, enjoyment, and curiosity, while providing a gateway to more advanced Latin American history courses.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Hispanic and native backgrounds of the Spanish Conquest; a description and analysis of the evolution of colonial institutions; the independence movements in Hispanic America. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The colonial inheritances which influenced national development; political and economic trends of the nineteenth century; revolutionary trends in the twentieth century; inter-American relations. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the history and culture of modern East Asia from approximately 1700 to the end of the 20th century. We will focus on the internal changes and external challenges faced by the people and governments of China, Japan, Korea, and Vietnam. Students in this course will pursue a greater knowledge and understanding of modern East Asian history and civilization through a combination of readings, lectures, videos, discussion and writing assignments. (AS)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the history and culture of modern East Asia from approximately 1700 to the end of the 20th century. We will focus on the internal changes and external challenges faced by the people and governments of China, Japan, Korea, and Vietnam. Students in this course will pursue a greater knowledge and understanding of modern East Asian history and civilization through a combination of readings, lectures, videos, discussion and writing assignments. (AS

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course is designed to instruct students in the research and writing skills specific to the discipline. Taught in a seminar format, the course is based on students' discussions and written and oral work.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course will explore the path of European history from the origins of civilization to 1348. Its principle elements include the early societies of Mesopotamia, Egypt and Israel, the political and cultural contributions of Greece and Rome, the rise of Christianity and Islam, the characteristics of the medieval world, and the Black Death. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course will explore the history of Europe in the early modern period, bracketed by the Black Death and the French Revolution. Principle themes include the artistic achievements of the Renaissance, the expansion of education and literacy, the invention of the printing press, the religious conflicts of the Reformation, the growth of centralized nation-states, the dramatic discoveries of the Scientific Revolution, and the creation of a global framework for the European experience. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: A survey of the history of Europe in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, which examines the development of the political, social and economic systems that characterize the modern world. This course will identify, explore, and define the developments of modern European history, question why they happened, and evaluate their impact. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: HIST 20603 covers the same era as HIST 10603 but emphasizes interdisciplinary themes of intellectual history developed in Honors Intellectual Traditions or Honors Western Civilization courses. The course will focus upon how ideas translated from the European experience to influence American history and helped create a distinctly American mind. Though a strong historical narrative will be evident, the course will include literature, politics and philosophy. (US)
courses.prereqText: HIST 20603 covers the same era as HIST 10603 but emphasizes interdisciplinary themes of intellectual history developed in Honors Intellectual Traditions or Honors Western Civilization courses.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Prerequisites: Honors standing. HIST 20613 covers the same era as HIST 10613 but emphasizes interdisciplinary themes of American intellectual history developed in Honors Intellectual Traditions or Honors Western Civilization courses. The course will focus upon how various ideas and issues within the American experience following the Civil War and national westward expansion influenced U.S. history and helped create a distinctly American culture and intellectual tradition. Though a strong historical narrative will be evident, the course will include literature, politics, sociology, religious studies, demography, and philosophy. (US)
courses.prereqText: Honors standing. HIST 20613 covers the same era as HIST 10613 but emphasizes interdisciplinary themes of American intellectual history developed in Honors Intellectual Traditions or Honors Western Civilization courses.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Traces the role of the armed forces in American society through a study of the origins and developments of military institutions, traditions, and practices. Traces principal wars, including their causes, course, and effects, and treats the effects of leadership and new technologies. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Through lectures, reading, classroom discussions, and research assignments, this course examines the indigenous, European, and African roots of Latin American civilization and culture; the evolution of colonial institutions and ideas; the emergence of a distinctly Latin American culture; and the independence movements that established national states in most of Spanish and Portuguese America by 1830. The course will also include some comparative analysis with other civilizations. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Through lectures, reading, classroom discussions, and research assignments, this course examines the civilization and culture of modern Latin America, including the formation of national states; continuing colonial economic and political characteristics; the impact of ideas on Latin American development; class struggle and conflict between socialist and capitalist models of development; and the emergence of distinctive Latin American and national cultures. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the history and culture of traditional Asia from Neolithic times to approximately 1500. We will focus on the major political, economic, cultural, religious and intellectual trends of the people of East, South and Southeast Asia. Students in this course will pursue a greater knowledge and understanding of Asian history and civilization through a combination of readings, lectures, videos, discussion, and writing assignments. (AS)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the history and culture of modern Asia from approximately 1500 to 1989. We will focus on the internal changes and external challenges faced by the people and governments of such East, South and Southeast Asian states as China, Japan, Korea, India, Pakistan, Indonesia and Vietnam. Students in this course will pursue a greater knowledge and understanding of modern Asian history and civilization through a combination of readings, lectures, videos, discussion and writing assignments. (AS)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course represents credit earned through a semester study abroad experience with an institution or program with which Texas Christian University has an official agreement to accept credit. The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Archaeological and cultural survey from pre-Greek beginnings to the Roman conquest of Greece. Emphasis on discovery of the Minoan and Mycenaean world, the origins of Greek civilization, life in the Greek city-state, the Greek world view, and the conquests of Alexander the Great. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Archaeological and cultural survey of the Roman world from its origins to the barbarian invasions. Emphasis on the origins of Rome, Roman imperialism and its impact on the Roman way of life, the Roman Revolution, the political absolutism of the empire, the historical Jesus and Christianity in the Roman context, and the decline and fall of the Roman Empire. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Archaeological and cultural survey of the ancient civilizations of Egypt and the Near East. Visual presentation of archaeological evidence is emphasized along with the origins of civilization, the life and death of civilization, comparison of different values and world views, the origin of monotheism, and the rise and decline of the Assyrian and Persian Empire. (ME)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: A survey of ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern history from the Paleolithic Age to the Fall of Rome, including ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Levant, Greece and Rome. The course examines in a scholarly manner various topics from this period to show the history of the interest and expose common misinformation. Typical mysteries considered are the fall of Rome, the historical Jesus, the pyramids, Biblical events, the Neanderthal problem, the search for the Trojan War. (NWH)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Public history internships provide valuable opportunities for students to acquire knowledge, apply skills, and gain practical experience in a wide range of history-related fields. These include (but are necessarily limited to) archives, museums, historic sites, historic preservation, oral history, and documentary editing.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course introduces students to public history and to jobs in institutions such as museums, state and national parks, archives, and other cultural entities. Topics covered: preserving and sharing the past for a general audience; interpreting sensitive historical topics; engaging the community through public history partnerships; finding employment in the field.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This women's studies and history cross-listed course will enhance students¿ understanding of women in African history. It will introduce students to diverse lived experiences, life stories, roles, and agency of African women against the backdrop of power systems.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: A political and cultural survey of medieval civilization in the period A.D. 500-1600 Topics of emphasis include the reign of Charlemagne, early Byzantine and Islamic civilization, feudalism and the code of chivalry, the manorial economy, the crusades, the conflict of state and church, the rise of towns and universities, the Hundred Years' War, and the Black Death. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Prerequisite: Junior standing as a history major and membership in the Honors Program; HIST 20003. An examination of a major issue in history. This course is only offered as a tutorial and the specific topic is determined by consultation with an instructor. Arrangements for this course must be made with an instructor the semester prior to enrollment. (NWH or WH)
courses.prereqText: Junior standing as a history major and membership in the Honors Program; HIST 20003. An examination of a major issue in history.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The political, social and cultural development of Europe from 1300 to 1517. Topics include the Black Death and its impact, politics and culture in the city-states, the social and economic bases of Renaissance society, the Renaissance in Northern Europe. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Europe in crisis? Topics include civil wars, social and religious instability, absolutism, the debate over the crisis of the seventeenth century. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: A new world in Europe. Topics include the spread of the Enlightenment, the role of intellectuals, social and political changes, challenges to the old order, the coming and impact of the American and French Revolutions. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines Spain's culture, politics, and society from its creation out of a collection of small medieval kingdoms to the age of Columbus and the creation of a colonial empire, the collapse of this empire in the nineteenth century, and the path from dictatorship to democracy in the 20th century. It will include an emphasis on the Spanish values and beliefs that generated periods of religious cooperation and repression, experiments in absolute monarchy and constitutional government, and an ongoing tension between the desire for national unity and the recognition of regional differences. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Prerequisites: HIST 10213 or equivalent is recommended. While traditional history courses focus on major political and economic trends and individuals, this course addresses the culture, beliefs, and activities of ordinary people: the peasants, artisans, and laborers who made up the vast majority of the population in early modern Europe (1300-1800). Topics include food and festivity, witchcraft, popular religion, death, sexuality, and crime. (EU)
courses.prereqText: HIST 10213 or equivalent is recommended. While traditional history courses focus on major political and economic trends and individuals, this course addresses the culture, beliefs, and activities of ordinary people: the peasants, artisans, and laborers who made up the vast majority of the population in early modern Europe (1300-1800).

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The nineteenth century ushered in the industrial age in Europe and the modern consumer society. This course will examine the economic, social, and political change that came with the process of industrialization. Topics include: workers, women, socialism, revolution, nationalism and unification, and imperialism. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: World War II was the second global conflict in two generations. This course will examine the events of the interwar years that precipitated World War II and the war's impact on Europe. Topics include: the Treaty of Versailles, the Great Depression, the rise of fascism and its national variations, the Resistance. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: World War II left Europe in ruins. This course will examine Europe's recovery from the war and its position in the post war world. Topics include: the economic miracle, the Cold War and its impact, decolonization and the European Union. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The 1789 French Revolution marked a watershed in modern world history. This course examines events from 1750 to 1815, exploring the origins of the Revolution, the shifts in the 1790s from constitutional monarchy to the Terror's radical republicanism to Napoleon's dictatorship. Topics include: the emergence of new ideas and new media; the roles of writers, working people, and women; the involvement of other countries, including America; the long term political and social consequences; historians; interpretations of the Revolution. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Traces the political, diplomatic, military, economic, and social events in Germany in the period. Topics include the impact of the French Revolution and Napoleon, the rise of nationalism, the social impact of industrialization, political unification under Bismarck, the two world wars and their effects on Germany, the division of Germany following World War II and its reunification. Includes recent developments in the Federal Republic. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Traces European thought and culture in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Topics include nationalism, industrialism, romanticism, naturalism, socialism, the search for place, and the rise of fascism. Includes key developments in literature and the arts. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This study-abroad course has as its focus the historical trajectories of Paris and Madrid in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and is taught in conjunction with ENGL 40553, Studies in Nineteenth-Century American Literature: American Writers in Paris and Madrid. The two courses together will explore the experience of travel to Europe for Americans in this period, the narratives they wrote about their travel, and the historical context of these experiences. With the cities of Paris and Madrid as a kind of traveling classroom to showcase the factual and physical context of these narratives, students in HIST 30383 will gain a familiarity with the principal historical developments surrounding Paris and Madrid in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the perceived and real differences between the two cities, and how this historical context shaped the experiences of the writers featured in the English course. This course will use historical sources alongside the literary texts of the English course as catalysts for studying the history and culture of their two cities. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines the most significant examples of the failure of nineteenth-century liberalism in Europe: the rise in the twentieth century of Stalin's Soviet Union, Hitler's Nazi Germany and Mussolini's Fascist Italy. Topics include a comparative analysis of their ideologies, their leaders' seizure of power, the initiatives and policies implemented at home and abroad, as well as the collapse of the Nazi and Fascist regimes and the survival of Stalin's Soviet system at least until his death. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The evolution of the early Russian state and its development under the Grand Princes and Czars to the emancipation of the serfs. Emphasis on the institutions, literature, religion, personalities, and cultural developments as well as major political events. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The forces and personalities that molded modern Russia after the emancipation of the serfs, the revolutionary movements and their leaders, and the economic and political factors that brought the downfall of the czarist regime. Special attention to the Marxist-Leninist doctrine and the Soviet attempt to implement it, Stalinism, the emergence of rival communist states, and the post-Stalin era. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The nationalist rivalries that led to Sarajevo, the cultural and economic conflicts that kept the Balkans divided, the problems faced by the region in the period following the First World War. Special attention to the struggle of the Czechs and the Poles to maintain their national existence despite threats from Hitler and Stalin. The effects of World War II on the region. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Explores the history of modern China, examining the major events and forces that have shaped the development of this important East Asian state. Topics include traditional Confucian society, the internal and external crises of the late imperial period, the revolution and attempts at state-building of the republican period, and the mass campaigns of the Maoist era.(AS)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: A survey of British history from pre-Roman times to the death of Elizabeth, emphasizing the constitutional, political, social, cultural, and economic developments. Special stress on the evolution of institutions and ideas which America and England share.(EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: A survey of the revolutionary developments in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries which brought the development of parliamentary government, social and political reform movements of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the transformation from Empire to Commonwealth, and the emergence of the welfare state. Britain's role as a world power will be examined and special emphasis will be given to the diplomatic developments that led to the two world wars. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Tudor-Stuart kings and their parliaments, emphasizing the English Reformation, the Elizabethan Age, the Puritan Revolution and Oliver Cromwell, the Restoration and the Glorious Revolution, and the rise of cabinet-political parties-civil rights struggles. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: An examination of the political, social and imperial themes in English history for the period 1815-1901, with emphasis on the impact of the Industrial Revolution, the new social order, demands for political reform, and the growth of British imperial power. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The major political, economic, imperial and intellectual developments of the period. Also discussed will be reforms, the rise of labor, and the impact of the two world wars. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Examination of Irish history from the plantations of the seventeenth century to the conclusion of the Troubles in the twentieth century. Particular attention will be given to the era of the penal laws, the place of Ireland within the British Empire, the development of a variety of forms of Irish nationalism, the causes and consequences of the Great Irish Potato Famine, the Anglo-Irish War and the partition of the island, and the struggle for civil rights and peace in Northern Ireland. The course will also introduce theories about colonial (and postcolonial) identities in modern Ireland. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Examination of the empire-building experience of Great Britain in the early modern period beginning with its experiences in Ireland, North America, and the Caribbean. Particular emphasis will be given to motivation, cultural collision, and the evolution of systems of control and administration. For the period following the American Revolution, the course will examine the development of new patterns of empire that emerge from the interplay of exploration, the missionary movement, the Napoleonic Wars and technological change. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Examination of the British Empire from its high-point in the second half of the Nineteenth Century to its dissolution after 1945. Particular attention will be given to the so-called New Imperialism and the scramble for African and Pacific territories, the place of empire in Victorian culture, the informal empire of economic investment, the impact of World War I on the imperial system, and the role of nationalism in the empire's eventual dissolution. The course will also introduce the theoretical arguments concerning the nature and function of the British Empire and its role in shaping the post-colonial world. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Focuses on experiences of ordinary men and women living in London during the past five hundred years. Examines the rise of London from its first period of rapid growth in the 1500s to its emergence as a multi-cultural and multi-racial city in the second half of the twentieth century. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This a course that combines lecture, discussion and field trips in order to introduce major themes and developments which have shaped English history. Although the course proceeds chronologically, emphasis will be placed on social structures and contexts rather than a timeline of events. The course is designed to take advantage of resources available in London; therefore, several classes will be held at sites such as Westminster Abbey, Parliament, Battle Abbey, and Bodiam Castle. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course analyzes the roles of women in American history since 1492. It examines the history of women in America primarily as they have intersected with the public realm - employment, politics, reform, war - but also considers women at home in their roles as daughters, wives, and mothers. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course analyzes the roles of working people in American history since the colonial period. It examines men and women in the various ways that they have made their livings, from farming to domestic work to manufacturing. The course pays particular attention to the way in which ethnicity has affected people's employment. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines the emergence of science as a way of knowing about the natural world and the human body in the period between 1450 and 1750, often referred to as the ¿Scientific Revolution.¿ We will analyze key figures and critical events in the evolution of physics, chemistry, astronomy, biology, and medicine by situating these figures and events within their social and cultural context. Students will confront popular myths about the relationship between science and religion in history to understand how science as a way of knowing has become synonymous with authority, truth, objectivity, and reason in contemporary society.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: In this course, students will explore the experiences of women in the history of Europe from 1789 to the present. Many of the topics and events will be familiar, industrialization, the French Revolution, the women's movement, the Russian Revolution, the World Wars, and the Cold War. Students will examine these events to investigate women's experiences and to discover women's contributions to the history of modern Europe. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course investigates changes in American food from European contact to the present. Topics will include the impacts of immigration and industrialization. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Explores Britain's nineteenth century through the career of Benjamin Disraeli, by turns novelist, dandy, romantic poet, Tory democrat, statesman, and twice prime minister. The story of how this middle-class, Jewish outsider became the ultimate political insider reveals the role of class, religion, and race in British society. Particular attention will be given Disraeli's role in the development of the British empire, the promotion of a modern monarchy, and democratization of the political system. (EU)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines the relationship between wars and societies. Course subject varies and could focus on specific wars, time periods, or nations. Additionally, the course could focus on such topics as the mobilization of militaries and civilian societies, the development of battlefield operations, the experiences of wartime societies and militaries, and the influence of such factors as culture, gender, technology, communication, and economics on wars. Students can take this course more than once as long as the course subjects are different.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This undergraduate seminar examines the ways in which societies from the ancient world to the present acquire, order, and assign value to material artifacts. From ethnographic remains to natural specimens, and from works of art to antiquities, people have plundered, collected, and displayed objects across time and space. Special attention to circulation will help students analyze the processes by which objects were detached from their natural context and reinserted into thematic sets based on aesthetic, religious, political or scientific priorities that gave rise to the modern museum. Topics include the culture of learning at the Library of Alexandria, relics and devotional practices in medieval Europe, collecting exotica during Renaissance, sensory museums of the Enlightenment, and black market trade of antiquities in the present. Class includes fieldtrips to local museums, libraries, and private collections.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: People who identify as queer have been integral to the history of the United States. We will examine the history of the US with attention to the experience of queer people. Queer people have always existed, more openly at some times than at others. We will trace the shifts in the ways that queer people have interacted with the public sphere and how American attitudes toward queerness have changed over centuries. We will examine primary sources--the actual words of the time. From those sources, the student makes an unfiltered connection to the people of the past.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course will ask how the ways that humans communicate¿via inscription, graffito, letter, or Tweet¿have the power to affect society and make history. We will explore the history of communications technologies from the invention of writing to the printing press to social media, and each week, we will pair these topics with analysis of a cutting-edge digital archive or project. Students will then learn how to use the ¿digital tools¿ reflected in these projects, building the skills necessary to produce their own works of digital historical scholarship.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: From the formation of the Egyptian state in the beginning of the 19th century until the current regime of President Mubarak, this course traces the struggle of Egyptian state and society to build a modern, but authentic, nation. The course addresses European imperialism, westernization, the rise of Arab nationalism, authoritarianism and political Islam among other forces that shaped the unique Egyptian experience. Social issues such as the formation of modern classes, women's position in society, and the contribution of minorities will be examined to understand continuity and change in Egyptian society. (ME)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the historical developments in Modern Iran that made its experience unique among Middle Eastern and Muslin nations. Students will learn how Iranian society, culture, and politics have evolved throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries to provide an appropriate historical context in which the 1979 Islamic Revolution took place and created the first Islamic Republic in the modern Middle East. (ME)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines the position, contribution, cultural representation and socio-economic status of women in the Middle East from the advent of Islam to the present with particular focus on the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. By tracing women's legal status, sexuality, public morality, family and social life, and female economic and political participation, this course seeks to shed light on the history of women in predominantly Muslin societies. (ME)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the historical developments of Syria and Iraq during the last hundred years, thus students will have a better understanding of the contemporary crisis that both states and societies are going through. Throughout the semester students will engage in learning through community services experience. Students will gain firsthand knowledge on the ongoing crisis through volunteering to provide services to Iraqi and Syrian refugees in Fort Worth community.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Comparative historical survey covering three great early-modern Muslim empires: the Mughals, the Safavids, and the Ottomans. The three empires ruled over a vast geography including North Africa, the Balkans, Turkey, the Arab Middle East, Iran, and the Indian Subcontinent. Major themes include the role of religion in early warriors' militancy, slave armies, early modern bureaucracy, the rise of Sunnism and Shi'ism as official religions as well as social status and gender relations.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: An introduction to U.S. urban history, focusing on race, space, community activism, labor, and urban politics from the Civil War to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This service-learning field research course introduces students to community-based research and oral history theory and methodology, including interviewing techniques and debates within the discipline. Students will conduct extensive independent research outside the comfortable confines of the university. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course surveys the history of the modern Chicano/a civil and immigration rights movement and explores Latino/a politics and immigration policy as ways to understand the nature of social movements and the role of grassroots activism; the connections between civil rights and other struggles for social justice, past and present; and the origins and persistence of structural racial and ethnic inequality in the United States. (Offered as POSC 31543 or HIST 30823 credit)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course surveys the history and politics of the modern African American civil rights movement and uses it as a vehicle to explore the theory and practice of group-centered leadership development; the nature of social movements and the role of grassroots activism; the connections between civil rights and other struggles for social justice, past and present; and the origins and persistence of structural racial inequality in the U.S. Credit not awarded for both POSC 31523 and HIST 30833.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This seminar covers the history of modern Afghanistan from its inception in the late nineteenth century to the "war on terror" in the twenty-first century. Themes covered include the history of the country during the "Great Game" between Britain and Russia, the history of modernization in the first half of the twentieth century, the Cold War, and the Soviet-American competition over the country, culminating in the Soviet invasion, the US support of the Islamist insurgency, the rise and demise of the mujahedeen and the Taliban, and finally the US war after 9/11.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines the intersection of racial (re)constructions and American law. Chronologically, the class covers a broad sweep of American legal history from the Founding era and into the 21st century. Students will examine the relationship between race, racial formation, creating inequality, boundaries, eliminating inequality, and legal practice in the U.S. Some thematic topics include slavery, the Constitution, Indigenous sovereignty, citizenship, immigration, and Jim Crow segregation.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Migration has been a prominent feature of human history worldwide, and the number of people who move¿whether to a different nation or to a city within their own country, temporarily or permanently, out of necessity or because they are forced to¿continues to rise. This course offers an overview of the history of migration within and across the Middle East and the Mediterranean region from the eighteenth century to the present. The major trends examined in class include early modern Mediterranean mobility, 19th-century colonial migration, the age of mass migration to the Americas, forced migration and population exchange projects in the 20th century, and the Mediterranean migration ¿crisis¿ of 2015.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines Native American movements in modern Latin America and their impact on conceptions of nation and citizenship, focusing on the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Survey of Central America from colonial times to the present with emphasis on the region's economic and political development and the emergence of revolutionary movements in the twentieth century. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Early diplomatic relations among the independent republics; the Monroe Doctrine in Hemispheric politics; the movement for Pan American union; the Big Stick and Dollar Diplomacy; the Good Neighbor Policy and the Alliance for Progress. (LA or US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Survey and analysis of revolutionary movements in modern Latin America, with special emphasis on Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Cuba, Mexico, and Central America. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The clashing and mingling of cultures in regions formerly held by Spain in the southeastern and southwestern United States. (US)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Southern South America from colonial times to the present; a comparison of the colonial experiences of both countries and their impact on national development; problems of modernization and the movements of social revolution. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The growth of the Brazilian nations and civilization from colonial plantation beginnings through experiments with monarch and republic, to the rank of major nation. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Courses dealing with problems and historical questions in a particular area of specialization. The topics will be changed from semester to semester and the course may be repeated when the topic is different. (3 hours NWH or WH)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Examination of a selected period of colonial or modern history through biography of prominent individuals. Individuals will include people such as Sor Juana or Fidel Castro although biographies and periods will vary with each semester. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: Investigation and analysis of the Indian Civilizations of Mexico, the Caribbean Region, Central and South America with particular emphasis on the Mayas, Aztecs, and Incas. Also discussed will be the impact of European culture on the native population and the contemporary problem of integrating the Indian into modern society. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: The native peoples, the Spanish Conquest and cultural conflict, evolution of colonial society, the movement for independence, 19th century efforts at modernization, revolutionary Mexico and U.S.-Mexican relations. (LA)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course examines the role of food in Latin American social, cultural, economic, political, and environmental life, since the fifteenth century. It centers Latin America within key transformations in the global history of food, from the Columbian Exchange to contemporary food sovereignty movements, and asks how those historical shifts impacted foodways. In this course, food is much more than lens of analysis; it is a hands-on and embodied experience that empowers us to engage all of our senses to advance our learning. Buen Provecho!

courses.subject: HIST
courses.description: This course is aimed at introducing participants to the cultural and socio-political development of Ghana through a four-week intensive, interdisciplinary study and travel-abroad experience in this West African nation. It is expected that participants will come away with a sense of the vast differences manifest in the way human societies work and, at the same time, develop a sincere respect for these differences. Course is open to students of all majors. Instructor's permission is required.
