courses.prereqText: Permission of department chair.

courses.subject: PORT
courses.description: A beginning course intended for students with no previous knowledge of the language. The skills of comprehension, speaking, reading, and writing are taught at the elementary level, with an emphasis on oral proficiency in everyday situations encountered in Portuguese-speaking countries. No prerequisite. (No credit given to native or heritage speakers.)

courses.subject: PORT
courses.description: Prerequisite: PORT 10103 or equivalent. Continued study of beginning Portuguese. (No credit given to native or heritage speakers.)
courses.prereqText: PORT 10103 or equivalent.

courses.subject: PORT
courses.description: Prerequisite: PORT 10203 or equivalent. Completion of the beginning-level survey of the Portuguese language. (No credit given to native or heritage speakers.)
courses.prereqText: PORT 10203 or equivalent. Completion of the beginning-level survey of the Portuguese language.

courses.subject: PORT
courses.description: Prerequisite: PORT 20103 or equivalent. Review, reinforcement, and integration of the skills at the beginning level. This course bridges the beginning level and the next level of intensive study. (No credit given to native speakers; heritage speakers may receive credit with permission of the department.)
courses.prereqText: PORT 20103 or equivalent.

courses.subject: PORT
courses.description: Prerequisites: SPAN 20203, 20213, or equivalent. Native Spanish speakers and heritage speakers are welcome with departmental approval. An intensive beginning Portuguese course designed for Spanish speakers and learners. The course focuses on the similarities and differences between Spanish and Portuguese, especially Brazilian Portuguese. The course comprehends basic vocabulary and fundamentals of grammar through practice in speaking, listening comprehension, reading and writing. The use of different media to explore cultural aspects of the Portuguese-speaking world is an integral part of the course.
courses.prereqText: SPAN 20203, 20213, or equivalent. Native Spanish speakers and heritage speakers are welcome with departmental approval.

courses.description: Prerequisites: PORT 20503 or equivalent. This course focuses on the language and culture of Brazil. Through exposure to authentic material such as essays, chronicles, short stories and film, students will use the Portuguese language to explore a variety of topics ranging from personal anecdotes to societal and cultural issues that are relevant to understanding Brazil. Class is taught entirely in Portuguese.
courses.prereqText: PORT 20503 or equivalent.

courses.description: Prerequisite: PORT 20203 or equivalent. A study of the cultural institutions, both historical and contemporary, that distinguish Brazilian society.

courses.description: The American political system at national and state levels, including a survey of the federal and Texas Constitutions. This course satisfies the Texas state certification requirements for education majors. Students cannot receive credit for both POSC 10133 and POSC 20123.

courses.description: Prerequisites: Prior completion of or concurrent enrollment in MATH 10043, MATH 10283 or MATH 10524. Introduction to political science as a field of study and to the major issues in relating theory and empirical research to the study of political behavior.
courses.prereqText: Prior completion of or concurrent enrollment in MATH 10043, MATH 10283 or MATH 10524. Introduction to political science as a field of study and to the major issues in relating theory and empirical research to the study of political behavior.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Introduction to the dynamics of American governmental institutions and political processes through the study of significant contemporary issues in the American political arena. The particular issues may vary from semester to semester in accordance with the changing interests of students and instructor. Students cannot receive credit for both POSC 20123 and POSC 20144 or for both POSC 20123 and POSC 10133.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: An introduction to the essential information and skills for individuals to become responsible participants in the civic lives of their communities. The course includes a laboratory segment in which students will participate in the development and implementation of group community projects. Students cannot receive credit for both POSC 20123 and POSC 20144.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Introduction to the normative or value dimensions of political inquiry through the study of selected classics in political literature.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Introduction to both the major actors and issues which comprise contemporary international politics. A major goal of the course is to familiarize students with non-western perspectives on international phenomena.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Introduction to the essential elements of U.S. law and how law interacts with politics in the American context. The judicial process, substantive concepts and constitutional law are all studied.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Introduction to the concepts, theories and literature that enable effective comparison of political phenomena cross-nationally. Both western and non-western examples are examined.

The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Identifies the rationales for democracy, contrasts the institutional variation among contemporary persistently democratic societies, examines rival explanations for this variation, and prepares the student for the development of a senior capstone project.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Student is studying away this semester with a Partner Program.

The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Topics related to the study of American political institutions, processes, behavior, and policy, such as Congress, the Presidency, political parties and elections, interest groups, social and defense policy, and Texas politics.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course focuses primarily on campaigns and elections for national offices (especially Congress), however comparisons are made with state and local situations when appropriate. The class surveys the significant components of elections and campaigns to illuminate the implications of changes in the recent past, and the impact of these changes on governance in the United States.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course examines the origin, content, and measurement of the American public's views toward political matters. Topics include the values that unite us; the controversies that divide us; the social, historical, and psychological roots of contemporary American public opinion; the science of polling; and the responsiveness of the government.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course is an overview of the factors that influence political participation with a focus on the United States and comparison to other democracies. Models of participation, the role of demographic characteristics, and the influence of the political system and culture are analyzed. Political participation is examined at the individual and aggregate levels.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: The course examines the psychological aspects of the political behavior of individuals, including the general public, elites, and activists. It analyzes their consequent political behaviors in various groups and institutional contexts. Topics may include the development and functioning of ideology, political communication, decision-making, perception, and the impact of experiences on psychological states and processes.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course looks at the organization, behavior, and impact of the U.S. Congress. Some of the topics that will be considered are the recruitment and election of members, congressional organization and procedures, legislative policy-making, executive-legislative relations, and congressional reform.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This class examines presidential leadership, the constitutional basis of presidential power, presidential elections, and presidential interactions with other branches of government.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course explores the relationship between Congress and the presidency. Topics include the effect of events and individual personalities upon the ebbing and flowing relationship that exists between the legislative and executive branches of our government, and the principle problems and achievements of the most recent presidential administrations.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course focuses primarily on American political parties and interest groups by comparisons are made with several other democracies. The historical development of political parties and their current organizational structure, strengths and weaknesses, and the role in elections and in governing are analyzed. The role of interest groups in shaping public policy and influencing electoral politics is also critically examined.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course shines a critical light on the American news media by explaining how political news is made, exploring its effect on political institutions and process, and critiquing its role in American democracy. Topics include ideological bias, press norms and constraints, corporate ownership, media effects, and new media.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This class is an overview of the policy process in the United States and includes analysis of major issues associated with domestic public policy, including elements of economic and social policy.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: In this class, the centrality of health care policy is examined. Topics covered include interest group behavior in health care, the core policies related to health care, and the challenges that remain in health care policy.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course examines how the United States responds to and is transformed by migration.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the public policy issue of human trafficking through analyzing the perspectives of the different stockholders of anti-trafficking policy, including law enforcement, prosecutors, policymakers, judges, bureaucrats, the public, competing interest groups, and victims. This course also has a service-learning component that allows students to directly engage with the issue through site visit and research opportunities with local NGOs working to combat human trafficking in North Texas.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the politics and policies of data science and "big data." Students will gain an understanding of how public policy is made, including the role of data in policymaking. Students will learn about the ethical, legal, and social implications of data science and big data, including issues such as privacy, informed consent, security, safety, bias, and workforce impacts.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course examines how the political system, through the policies it establishes and enforces, affects those who identify as female and their families. It also examines the role of gender and sexuality in the political arena itself. The course considers what public policy is and how sex, gender, and sexuality impact legal, political, and social rights.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course surveys the history and politics of the modern African American civil rights movement and uses it as a vehicle to explore the theory and practice of group-centered leadership development; the nature of social movements and the role of grassroots activism; the connections between civil rights and other struggles for social justice, past and present; and the origins and persistence of structural racial inequality in the U.S. Credit not awarded for both POSC 31523 and HIST 30833.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course is about identity politics in the United States, which is a complex interdisciplinary topic that covers issues of race, gender, class, religion, age, and myriad of other identities that are core to human self-concept. As such, the course is divided into three sections. First, we will cover the central theories of identity in sociology and social psychology that have been used by political scientists to understand political phenomenon. The second section of the course will critically examine specific identities - those that have received disproportionate attention in political science literature - in light of the identity theories. The final section of the course will reflect on proposed strategies for best handling the oft-contentious nature of identity politics in a diverse democratic society.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course surveys the history of the modern Chicano/a civil and immigration rights movement and explores Latino/a politics and immigration policy as ways to understand the nature of social movements and the role of grassroots activism; the connections between civil rights and other struggles for social justice, past and present; and the origins and persistence of structural racial and ethnic inequality in the United States. (Offered as POSC 31543 or HIST 30823 credit)

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: The course introduces students to the dynamics of race in American political life. By focusing on African Americans, the course examines the foundations of Black politics, Black political behavior, and coalitions, movements, interest groups, parties, and elections.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: The course introduces students to the political experiences of Black women in the United States. The course examines these broad themes: foundations of Black Feminist Thought, understanding Black women political elites and self-care and self-preservation as an act of political warfare. We will read various authors of articles and book chapters that will situate Black women's identities, their unique experiences, and the impact these aspects have on their politics. We will examine how their politics differ from other Americans. We will explore the scholarship of Black women that is often not recognized in political science and how the discipline could benefit from their viewpoints.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Race, Class, and US Policing covers the politics and policy involving the surveillance, criminalization, policing, and incarceration of people in the United States, with special attention paid to the role of race and class.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This class examines Texas Politics in a comparative perspective. We will examine Texas's historical role in the national government, its constitution, politics and policies alone and in comparison to other states, and its political environment.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course provides a broad survey of the political, economic, and social issues and challenges confronting American cities and metropolitan areas. Major topics include the historical development of cities and governance; theories of urban politics and power; urban economic development; demographic changes; race and ethnicity; metropolitan growth patterns; and select contemporary urban public policies.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Architecture of democracy is about storytelling. In this class we will explore the politics, meaning, and behavioral impact of public architecture, both in terms of stories told by the built environment, and also by telling the stories of places and their meaning. Storytelling is important to the study, science and practice of politics. Data inform; stories persuade. The built environment has for millennia served, alongside the oral tradition, as humanity's most durable medium for storytelling, persuasion and the modification of human behavior.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: The class will examine the perennial dilemmas between freedom, order and equality especially as they pertain to political ideology and public policy. To understand the dilemmas, we will examine the basic structure of our government with special attention paid to the structural tensions that augment these dilemmas. Next we will look at how the dilemmas surface in contemporary debate among liberals and conservatives and how the dilemmas impact the definition of policies in the United States.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This class examines how science fiction enhances our ability to analyze politics, particularly through the use of counterfactuals and forecasting. By examining a variety of science fiction short stories, movies, and series, students learn how to critically analyze several public policy challenges for American government, including citizenship, immigration, the role of intelligence and expertise in policymaking, and the international challenge of failed states.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: In this course, we investigate what it means both theoretically and in practice to have a system of separated powers. Topics include how the legislative, executive, judiciary, bureaucracy, and state governments interact with each other. We explore why and how the different branches of government control discrete areas of power while also sharing overlapping authority.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This study abroad class will explore the political, economic, and social factors that influence the State Department in writing the Trafficking in Persons Report. Students will investigate these issues using India as a case study. Trough meetings with U.S. Government officials in India, Indian government officials, Indian NGOs, and international organizations, students will gain an understanding of the complexity of foreign policymaking and learn about the sensitive interplay between the U.S. government and foreign governments, NGOs, and international organizations in shaping foreign policy.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: Junior Standing. This class broadly covers the history and structure of the U.S. intelligence community. We will study the history of intelligence collection in the U.S. from George Washington to the present and learn about the structure of the Central Intelligence Agency and the functions of the different units. We will also grapple with the challenges, tradeoffs, and ethics of intelligence collection in a democratic society that values transparency, accountability, and human rights
courses.prereqText: Junior Standing.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course represents credit earned through a semester study abroad experience with an institution or program with which Texas Christian University has an official agreement to accept credit. The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20203. Topics will be selected from varying periods of Western history: ancient, medieval, modern, and contemporary. Topics may focus on individual thinkers (Hobbes), groups of thinkers (the Liberal Tradition), or on policy questions (Human Nature and Public Policy or Assessing Normative Theories of Politics.)
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20203. The course examines new directions in political thought that emerged with the Renaissance and the Reformation, and traces the development of modern political theory through the Enlightenment. Attention is given to the relationship between theory innovation and "modernizing revolutions."
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisite: POSC 20203. Examines contrasting concepts of distributive justice and their rival theoretical bases from Aristotle to the present.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20203. This course examines what it means to apply rival general ethical systems (i.e., consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics) in everyday life, contrasting the relative strengths and weaknesses of these distinctive conceptions of ethics in the process.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisite: POSC 20203. What would a just society look like? Students examine libertarian, liberal, and socialist answers to this question. Authors assigned typically include Rawls, Noziek, Marx, and others, with an emphasis on contemporary thinkers and debates. Attention is paid to the implications of various theories of justice for practical policy issues such as taxation, income inequality, the size and scope of government services, and moral limits of the market.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20203. Students investigate global institutions and international relations from an ethical point of view. Topics include just war theory, global democracy, immigration, and global distributive justice. Readings drawn mainly from contemporary sources. Representative authors include John Rawls, Michael Walzer, and Peter Singer.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20203. Democracy is a global catchword today-but its meaning is contested and changing. This course provides a lucid overview of major theories of democracy, including liberal, pluralistic and participatory versions together with critical evaluations from inside and outside the west.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20203. This course offers a critical assessment of the History of Political Thought by means of exploring the concept of violence within a wide variety of contexts: carceral, institutional, legal, familial, colonial, neoliberal, and others.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20203. The course offers an important contribution to learning political theories and concepts form an interdisciplinary perspective, particularly in this globalized and interconnected world. CPT scholars study the political thought of non-western political traditions, exploring the ontological and epistemological assumptions that undergird differently situated political perspectives.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20203.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course traces the development of political theory from Greek antiquity through the medieval period. Through close analysis of key philosophical texts by Greek and Christian thinkers, students will learn about the foundations of Western political thought.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: 'Making Modern America: The American Ideal' teaches the importance of American virtues and values in a free marketplace of ideas. On a topic by topic basis, students examine limited government, capitalism, patriotism, tolerance, individualism, free speech, ethical citizenship, and the pursuit of happiness, looking at both their foundations and contemporary value. Students will analyze contemporary challenges to the American ideal, to serve as a basis for discussion and critique of the concept of an American Ideal through the end of the Modern Era in 1945.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course represents credit earned through a semester study abroad experience with an institution or program with which Texas Christian University has an official agreement to accept credit. The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Topics studied include such areas as foreign policy, globalization, international political economy, diplomacy and bargaining, and various regional issues.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Permission of the instructor. This course is the first of a two-part series of classes for students participating in Model United Nations. Students will study the history of the United Nations, UN institutions, and current issues that the UN addresses. Students are expected to critically analyze the factors that lead to both successful and unsuccessful action by the UN.
courses.prereqText: Permission of the instructor.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Permission of the instructor. This course is the second of a two-part series of classes for students participating in Model United Nations. Students will engage in primary-source research on international issues as assigned by the course instructor from the perspective of a country also assigned by the instructor.
courses.prereqText: Permission of the instructor.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This class is a theoretical examination of interstate (international) and intrastate (civil) war. In particular, the class will examine whether or not the factors that lead states to fight wars are related to the factors that lead states to negotiate an end to conflicts. After a theoretical introduction to the causes of war and peace, the class will draw on historic and present conflicts to evaluate the various theoretical explanations presented in class.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: The objective of this course is to examine the theories of International Relations through a gender-sensitive lens that takes into consideration the role of feminist theory and the positions of women. Throughout the semester students will discover what it means to use gender as a lens for viewing and understanding the world, and how that lens can be used to deconstruct issues of power.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Globalization is often used to describe the increasing interconnectedness of the world in terms of communication, culture, economics, politics, and technology. This course examines the origins and dilemmas associated with globalization and the transnational institutions established to cope with this process. In addition, we will discuss the various theories with regard to globalization and its effects on international political economy.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course is designed to provide a forum for analysis and discussion of some of the most significant and vexing issues of global politics and political economy in the post-Cold War and the Post-Modern era in the context of globalization, and the intellectual debates surrounding it. Some of the concepts discussed include globalization, environmental degradation, the impact of high-tech and global economic interdependence, inequality, migration, hybrid identity and religious revivalism.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course will introduce students to issues surrounding energy, global political economy and global geo-strategy. Through historical analysis, students will reflect on the significant role that energy has played in charting the political map of the twentieth century and continues to shape political and economic events today. Students will investigate and explore the role of fossil fuels, unconventional resources, renewables and other alternative source of energy, while discussing their cost-effectiveness, environmental impact and viability to satisfy the increasing global demand for energy. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify, define and analyze pertinent issues surrounding global energy security and environmental sustainability.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course is designed to be an introduction to the political economy of human trafficking where students will spend two weeks studying abroad with site-enhanced visits. We will meet with government officials and representatives from local NGOs who will discuss some of the factors contributing to human trafficking and will engage in service learning activities that give students hands on experience in the three P's of human trafficking: prevention, prosecution and protection. Through these experiences students will gain a better understanding of the political and economic factors that contribute to the growth of human trafficking around the globe.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Examines contemporary challenges and opportunities for U.S. foreign policy.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Examines the processes by which U.S. foreign policy is made and the actors and motivations involved.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Examines the major events shaping U.S. foreign policy from the end of World War II to the present. The course augments a traditional lecturer and discussion format with the use of selected feature films to convey an emotional understanding of the period under study.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: The course will examine modern day international responses to the emergency needs of people damaged by both major disasters and by the multitude of inter and intra state conflicts that have arisen in much of the world since the end of the Cold War.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course serves as an introduction to the international relations (IR) of East Asia. We will begin with an introduction to Asia's distinct historical and cultural traditions and review some of the commonalities that can be drawn across states in the region. Next, we will focus on some of the key actors in Asia - China, Japan, North and South Korea - examining how they interact with each other as well as how they engage other important actors such as the US. Finally, we will examine economic development, institutions, and security concerns as they relate to the strategic interests of the region and individual states.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course examines Japan's relationship with the rest of the world. We begin with a focus on World War Two, but most of the class focuses on Japan's postwar relationships, as they relate to trade, international security, and international norms.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course will examine China's foreign relations from the founding of the People's Republic of China (PRC) in 1949 to the present. We will explore the theories and concepts involved in the study of foreign policy, followed by an in-depth examination of the domestic factors shaping China's foreign policy goals and implementation.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Examines Russian foreign policies and how and why particular policies are (or have been) formulated and implemented from the end of the Cold War to the present.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Examines the major conflicts shaping the modern Middle East, from the 1890s to the present and seeks to understand these conflicts, their root causes, and the possibilities for peace in the region.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: The course sequence includes Judicial Process, International Human Rights, and several courses on American Constitutional Law. A simulation of the U.S. Supreme Court may be offered in alternate years.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: An overview of the Supreme Court as a political institution and its role in defining the limits of power among the three branches of the national government and between the states and the national government.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: An overview of the 4th Amendment (searches and seizures,) the 5th Amendment (double jeopardy, privilege against self-incrimination and federal due process of law), the 6th Amendment (speedy trial, confrontation of witnesses, and right to counsel), the 8th Amendment (excessive bail, cruel and unusual punishment, and the 14th Amendment (state due process.)

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: An overview of the rights of the First Amendment, including speech, press, religion, association, assembly and petition.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: An overview of cases involving categorical discrimination under the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course explores how courts abroad operate, including organization of courts, selection and appointment mechanisms, judicial independence, judicial review, human rights and the role of courts in the larger political system.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: An overview of rights recognized under the principle of customary law and under several international or transnational covenants and conventions.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Must be selected as a member of the TCU Intercollegiate Moot Court Team. Appellate advocacy involving cases taken from the current or recent dockets of the Supreme Court of the United States, as well as the current case problem set by the American Collegiate Moot Court Association. This course may be repeated once for credit.
courses.prereqText: Must be selected as a member of the TCU Intercollegiate Moot Court Team.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This constitutional law course explores how the Supreme Court has defined and applied the rights contained in Amendment I, Amendment XIV and other rights implied from the first nine amendments. The focus is on the Court as a policy-making branch of the U.S. government.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: An overview of law, courts and politics in the United States and the various theories that have been proposed to explain decision-making by judges, prosecutors, law enforcement and juries.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: European politics, Asian politics, Latin American politics, Middle Eastern politics, developing political systems, etc.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Examines the rationales for democracy, contrasts the institutional variation among contemporary persistently democratic societies, and introduces rival explanations for this variation.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Why do people join together in protest, often at great cost to themselves in money, time, and/or risk of serious personal injury? This course will examine this and other questions related to social movement organization, strategy, and impact. It will look at these questions on a theoretical level and as they apply to a variety of real world social movements in different national contexts.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course presents a study of Islam and politics. It attempts to shed light on how Islamic theology molds and provides legitimacy for political discourse of resistance as well as power politics. More specifically, the focus is on politics of Islam and how it sets the political agenda. Among topics of interest would be a discussion of Islam and terrorism, Islam and Human rights, and the prospects for relations between the Muslim World and the West.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course focuses on the political problems associated with development: the problems of poverty, economic development - the colonial heritage, economic dependence, and the character of the Third World state; the problems of political development - clientelism, corruption, and centralized state power; and the problem of establishing a stable form of government - transition from authoritarian rule, democracy, liberalization and democratization.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course would present a historical analysis of the rise and decline of the Middle East. We would stress power and authority relationships, the role of political culture in evolution of regional politics. Special emphasis will be placed upon the capacity of Middle Eastern political systems to confront the related challenges of modernization, political development and democratization.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: In this course we examine Japanese politics and society through both the scholarship of those who have dedicated their lives to studying Japan and through films (mostly films made by and for Japanese audiences.) Ultimately, we will strive to understand how Japanese politics and society work and to use this understanding to deepen our sense of how politics and societies function more generally.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This class will introduce students to Japan's postwar political system. In addition to learning how the political system works in the abstract, we also examine the way that the political system has actually functioned, particularly in regards to the relationship between the state and society, economic governance, and foreign policy.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course will examine the social, economic and institutional elements that shape the politics of the People's Republic of China. The issues covered in the course include: political culture, civil society, political elites, democracy, development, and environmental politics.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course is designed to be an introduction to Chinese history, politics, economics, and civilization where students will spend two weeks in China with site-enhanced visits. The primary locations are Beijing and Shanghai, where students will have an opportunity to visit the Forbidden City, Summer Palace, Lama Temple and several other sites to see how the country blends tradition with modernization. Through these experiences students will gain a better understanding of China and see how one of the world's most rapidly developing countries is adjusting to the demands of globalization.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course will examine the development of an entrepreneurial mindset in modern China, focusing on the period from 1949 to the present. The course covers the history of entrepreneurship in China and how market reforms introduced in the post-1978 era helped inspire creativity, innovation, and the creation of new values among the Chinese. This transition to an economic model which the Chinese refer to as socialism with Chinese characteristics, has transformed China both economically and politically.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course introduces students to the various institutions, political cultures and decision-making apparatus of the nations of Western Europe and the European Union.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: An exploration of the creation and functioning of the European Union and its effects on politics of the Member States.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course is onsite, and is offered as a part of the TCU Summer study abroad program. It is intended to provide a forum for discussion and analysis of post-Communist transition in Hungary and Czech Republic since the 1989 revolution that overthrew Communism.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: Upper division standing. This site-enhanced study abroad course would focus on the study of economic transition in Hungary, Czech Republic and Croatia since the revolution of 1989 that toppled Communism in these countries. We would study the process of privatization of formerly state-owned enterprises and the building of a market economy and Capitalism with "a comrade face". We would also study the economic impact of European Union Accession on these countries and overcoming the challenges of corruption and the creation of a social safety net.
courses.prereqText: Upper division standing.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course offers an examination of monarchy, democracy, and authoritarianism through the medium of film and television.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course offers an introduction to the domestic and international politics of the United Kingdom.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: The course examines key factors (patterns of conquest, inter-American relations) that have shaped Latin American politics historically and then focuses concentrated attention to the factors that affect Third Wave democratization in the region. Much of the course is centered on case studies.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: Any upper division course. In this course, we conduct a case study of central European nations, considering the geo-economics and geo-politics of energy transition and the collective striving toward a sustainable future. We investigate the implications for the US of lessons learned from the Central European experience, the challenges the US faces, and possible pathways to overcoming them. This site-enhanced course provides a forum for discussion and analysis of these issues from a multidisciplinary perspective, drawing from the insights of political science, sociology, and local experts on sustainability.
courses.prereqText: Any upper division course.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20093 or consent of the instructor. Topics include political science methods applied to various research problems such as political behavior, public policy analysis, and program evaluation.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20093 or consent of the instructor.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20093, MATH 10043 or its equivalent. This is a course that will study the use of surveys in political science. Students will learn to assess surveys for their quality, to write a survey, to take the survey from concept to fruition, to analyze survey data, and to write a research paper from the analysis they do.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20093, MATH 10043 or its equivalent.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20093. This class is designed as a workshop to introduce students to the use of game theory in international relations. The first part of the class will provide students with basic instruction on game theory and formal models, including how to create a decision tree, how to find equilibrium points in a game, and how to design a basic game. The second part of the class will be a writing workshop as students progress in their original research and writing in pursuit of a written project that incorporates formal methodology.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20093.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20093. Teaches the skills associated with traditional decision-making analysis applied to a foreign policy setting.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20093.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisite: POSC 20093. This course is about case study research - the study of a set of events bounded by space and time. Its emphasis is on how to formulate research questions and design research strategies for the rigorous application of social science standards and logics of inference in those instances where the empirical evidence involved is primarily qualitative rather than quantitative, and where a limited number of cases can and should be studied in significant detail.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20093.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20093. This class is an introduction to the use of experimental methodology in political science. Students will compare experimental methods to other methods of social scientific inquiry, and learn about the core concepts in experimental design. Students will then design, field, and analyze data from their own experiments and produce an original research paper by the end of the semester.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20093.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20093. This course introduces you to two related qualitative research methodologies--interview research and ethnography--as used in social sciences in general and in political science in particular. Although these two research methodologies differ in a number of important way, what unites them is that in order to use both techniques well, the researcher is required to have long, open-ended conversations with research subjects.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20093.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: This course represents credit earned through a semester study abroad experience with an institution or program with which Texas Christian University has an official agreement to accept credit. The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 20093. This course is designed to prepare students to conduct original research generally and to complete an undergraduate thesis specifically. The course lays the groundwork for the formulation, design and completion of an original research project. Through seminars and project assignments, students work through the identification of a research question to the preparation of a specific research design to complete the project, with appropriate training in the techniques and strategies at each stage. Student work culminates in the completion of a research proposal that is presented for approval by a faculty committee, which then leads to the completion of the thesis during the subsequent semester.
courses.prereqText: POSC 20093.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: POSC 30003 or 40093, and 40001. The writing of a substantial research paper under the supervision of a three person faculty committee. A grade of Incomplete will be carried in this course until the paper is completed.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Membership in good standing in the department's Distinction Program. Identifies the rationales for democracy, contrasts the institutional variation among contemporary persistently democratic societies, examines rival explanations for this variation, and prepares the student for the development of a senior capstone project.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Washington Center or at the TCU in London Program. Full-time internships with a public or private agency in Washington, D.C. or in London, England, offered either through the Washington Center or through the TCU in London Program. The internship will allow students to integrate theory and practice in a supervised professional setting, up to 12 semester hours credit. (Offered as BRST or POSC credit.)

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Full time internships with a public or private agency in Washington, D.C. offered in collaboration with the Washington Center. Offered during the Fall term only, these internships help students to integrate theory and practice in a supervised professional setting for up to 12 semester hours credit.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: 3-day or 4-day per week interns with public or private agencies in London, England, offered through the TCU in London Program. Offered during the fall and spring terms, these internships accommodate students' long-term professional objectives. Internships are offered for either 9 or 12 semester hours credit. Most of the London interns also take one or two classroom courses while in London. (Offered either for BRST or POSC credit.)

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Individually arranged local internship for 3 semester hours credit. Students expected to spend 150 hours in a local placement (in a regular term that would amount to 10 hours per week.) (This course is only offered as P/NC.)

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: These are supervised internships in local settings, with bi-weekly meetings to reflect on a variety of experiences of the students. Students are expected to spend 150 hours in a local placement (in a regular term that would amount to 10 hours per week.) (This course is only offered as P/NC.)

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisite: A specific program of study approved by instructor prior to enrollment. (1-6 semester hours)
courses.prereqText: A specific program of study approved by instructor prior to enrollment.

courses.subject: POSC
courses.description: Prerequisites: 6 hours of POSC coursework completed. Exploration of career options and career readiness for political science majors. This course will guide students to explore career options, identify career paths and relevant experiences, develop skills (e.g., interviewing techniques, adopting professional attitudes and behavior), and engage in resume building and career mentoring.
courses.prereqText: of POSC coursework completed. Exploration of career options and career readiness for political science majors.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Transfer work with TCUCC-NSC credit.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Freshman or sophomore standing or consent of the instructor. The study of the skills and techniques necessary for efficient learning. Application of the principles of learning, cognition, and motivation to the problems of college learning. This class is offered for 3 hours credit.
courses.prereqText: Freshman or sophomore standing or consent of the instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: One of the prerequisites for higher-level psychology courses. An introduction to the science of psychology, including basic brain and behavioral processes, memory and cognition, human development, social behavior, and psychological disorders. Integrates biological, social, cognitive, and learning influences on behavior and addresses the role of cultural differences and diversity. Credit cannot be given for both PSYC 10213 and either 10514 or 10524.
courses.prereqText: for higher-level psychology courses.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: General Psychology, with no CORE designation.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Recommended for B.S. in Psychology. An introduction to the scientific study of behavior. The nature of scientific inquiry of behavior and relevant basic behavioral processes will be discussed. Three hours lecture and two hours laboratory per week. Credit cannot be given for both PSYC 10213 and 10514.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Recommended for B.S. in Psychology. An introduction to the scientific inquiry of behavior. The nature of scientific inquiry of behavior and relevant behavioral processes will be discussed. Three hours lecture and two hours laboratory per week. Credit cannot be given for both PSYC 10213 and 10524.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Transfer work

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Transfer work

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524. This course explores career paths in psychology, including careers requiring undergraduate and graduate degrees in psychology. Additional topics include choosing coursework that matches student career goals and learning skills to help students be a successful job or graduate school applicant.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: This course will evaluate current issues involved in choice, including the debate between determinism and free will, and the paradox of choice. The course aims to provide an appreciation of the interplay between theory and empirical research. This course will cover questions like when we choose, how we choose, and why we regret from a psychological perspective. The goal is for the student to gain a greater appreciation and understanding of the factors that influence choice and choice satisfaction.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Sophomore standing. Students will explore answers to fundamental questions about the psychology of leadership. Emphasis is on psychological theories and how they address the issue of "self-leadership". Psychological approaches to the measurement of leadership effectiveness will be used to critically evaluate various contemporary models found in popular culture.
courses.prereqText: Sophomore standing.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Teaches students how to think critically about the psychological research on romantic attraction and close relationships. The course goal is to educate intelligent consumers of media information and misinformation, teaching them to separate scientifically valid from invalid claims about the causes and consequences of initial romantic attraction, deepening close relationships, sex differences, problems that occur within close relationships, and effective versus ineffective strategies for resolving conflicts in close relationships.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: This course represents credit earned through a semester study abroad experience with an institution or program with which Texas Christian University has an official agreement to accept credit. The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Junior standing and membership in the Honors Program. An examination of a major issue in psychology. This course is only offered as a tutorial and the specific topic is determined by consultation with an instructor. Arrangements for this course must be made with an instructor the semester prior to enrollment.
courses.prereqText: Junior standing and membership in the Honors Program. An examination of a major issue in psychology.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524. An overview of contemporary knowledge about various states of consciousness including both theoretical perspectives and contemporary applications.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524. The nature of scientific theories and their application to the claims of paranormal events. The emphasis is on a skeptical analysis of such reputed phenomena as extra sensory perception, psychokinesis, clairvoyance, and precognition. Alternative explanations of claims of the paranormal using established scientific principles, laws and theories of behavior are examined.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524. Psychological Foundations of Education is a foundational course that explores the principles, theories, and research related to how people learn, develop, and are motivated within educational settings. Through a study of classic and contemporary theories of learning and development, including behaviorist, cognitive, and sociocultural perspectives, students will examine the complex interactions between cognitive, emotional, social, and cultural factors that influence the teaching and learning process.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Two hours lecture and three hours lab. Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, or approval of instructor. Instruction and practice in the elements of effective participation in task oriented groups and in the strategies and techniques of systematic problem solving. Topics in group processes include group membership roles, task oriented roles, leadership roles, group norms, competition, and conflict management. Topics in problem solving include problem definition, brainstorming, means-end analysis, and structured decision making.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, or approval of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524. This course will explore the music and life of Taylor Swift through the lens of psychological theories and research.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524. This course explores the stages of development, including infancy, early and middle childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and the end of life, from a lifespan perspective of human development, including physical, cognitive, and psychosocial changes.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524. Human behavior from conception to adolescence; the influences of heredity and maturation, physical, social and cognitive development, with child observations.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher. Methods and principles related to the experience and behavior of individuals in interaction with each other, in group situations, and in relation to items in the sociocultural setting. Credit cannot be given for both PSYC 30343 and PSYC 30353. .
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524. Methods and principles related to the experience and behavior of individuals in interaction with each other, in group situations, and in relation to items in the sociocultural setting. Credit cannot be given for both PSYC 30343 and PSYC 30353.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524 and junior standing. Course formerly named Abnormal Psychology. Personality and behavior processes in normal and deviant personalities; variations and causes of psychopathology, problems of classification, diagnosis and management.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524 and junior standing.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, or approval of instructor. Analysis of methods, accumulated knowledge, and systematic approaches to problems of group behavior in organizations including personnel management, selection, training, motivation, performance appraisal, leadership, working conditions, and human engineering.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, or approval of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213, 10514, or 10524. An exploration of various forms of oppression, including racism, sexism, ageism, heterosexism, and inclusivity at various levels will be addressed.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 30503. This class will teach students the fundamental principles of evolution and show how these principle can be used to provide new insights into human social behavior. Examples of topics to be covered are emotions, motivation, sexual attraction, parenting, aggression, and status-seeking. This course has a written component.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher. Three lectures and one laboratory per week. Basic methods and concepts employed in the study of learning.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503, at least one of the following: PSYC 10514, PSYC 30463, or PSYC 30483, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher. Two lectures and one laboratory period per week. Basic experimental techniques employed in the study of detection, discrimination and recognition of visual and auditory stimuli.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503, at least one of the following: PSYC 10514, PSYC 30463, or PSYC 30483, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503. Basic concepts, theories, and techniques employed in the study of motivation.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524. The factual and theoretical status of the development, structure, and dynamic functioning of the adult personality.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503. An overview of major issues and topics in modern cognitive psychology with particular emphasis on interpreting basic research in memory and cognitive processes. Credit cannot be earned for both PSYC 30453 and PSYC 30523.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524 or approval of instructor. Study of the nervous system, action systems, and sensory systems to provide background for examining the physiological bases of discrimination, motivation, emotions, and learning. (Crosslisted as BIOL/PSYC 30463.)
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524 or approval of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 30503. Provides knowledge of animal behavior as a field of research based on mechanistic and evolutionary approaches. Provides a basic vocabulary and a conceptual framework which enables the student to appreciate the importance and scope of animal behavior as an interdisciplinary field and to identify areas of interest for further study.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, or approval of instructor. Presents an approach to the study of human brain function by examining the behavioral syndromes resulting from neurological disease and brain damage. Topics will include an overview of the nervous system; neuropsychological assessment; cortical dysfunction; language disorders; developmental neuropsychology; and recovery of function following brain trauma.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, or approval of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, plus MATH 10043. Basic elements of research methods used in psychological science including research-planning, execution, analysis, and interpretation. This course introduces the selection of research questions, measurement of physiological, behavioral, and psychological constructs, development of research procedures, and experimental and non-experimental designs as well as the basic statistical methods and concepts needed in psychological science.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, plus MATH 10043.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503. This course is concerned with the discipline of learning psychology and its application to the study of behavior in human and non-human animals. We will not, however, be directly concerned with methods and issues in Educational or Applied branches of Psychology. IN this course, learning is the informal process by which we learn to adapt our behaviour through experience. Students will become familiar with concepts and theory related to how this type of learning is achieved. This course will include empirical research on topics such as reflexes, orienting mechanisms, associative conditioning (Pavlovian and instrumental), memory processes, stimulus control, and choice behavior.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher. This class will meet for three hours of lecture and two hours of laboratory per week. Topics for this course include gaining an appreciation for experimental cognitive psychology - the study of how knowledge is acquired, represented, and maintained. Major findings and current thinking about a broad range of topics in experimental cognitive psychology will be discussed in the areas of attention, memory, language, decision-making, and reasoning among others. Credit cannot be given for both PSYC 30524 and PSYC 30453.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 30414 or 30433 or 30453 or 30473 or 30513. This course will evaluate current issues of animal cognition, including memory, tool use, numerical sense, theory of mind, navigation, and language. This course aims to provide an appreciation of the interplay between theory and empirical research. This course will begin with a discussion of empirical research on reflexes, orienting mechanisms, and associative conditioning (Pavlovian and instrumental) to provide a framework for applying knowledge of basic learning processes to claims of higher-order cognition.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: MATH 10043. Introduction to the process of evaluating data from psychological research using descriptive and inferential statistics as tools. The primary focus is on connecting psychological theory, research design, and basic statistical techniques. An emphasis will be placed on practical data skills, data visualization, use of statistical software, and the interpretation and communication of findings.
courses.prereqText: MATH 10043.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: Junior standing or instructor approval. The course is an introduction to research findings, theory, and application of Positive Psychology in a cross-cultural environment. From a positive psychology perspective, students will identify and employ individual character strengths, analyze decision -making processes that allow individuals and communities from different cultures to thrive, and evaluate the impact of service learning.
courses.prereqText: Junior standing or instructor approval.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, and PSYC 30503. The roots of modern psychology and the development of the schools of psychology will be discussed. The historical developments in science and philosophy that were the determinants of the founding of psychology will be analyzed.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience or Child Development major, and junior standing and higher. This course provides an in-depth analysis of the development of social relationships, behaviors, and emotions. Students will be introduced to topics such as temperament, attachment, emotion regulation, peer relationships, morality, aggression, and parenting.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience or Child Development major, and junior standing and higher.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 30503. This course will examine the nature of creativity through scientific study. Topics include major domains of creativity, the cognitive processes and neural structures involved in being creative, and how to improve creative thinking in everyday life.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prereq: PSYC 10213, 10514, or 10524 AND PSYC 30503. This writing emphasis course will examine the connection between psychological concepts and video games. Topics include the influence of video games on behavior and mental processes, psychological mechanisms in video game design and development, and the incorporation of video games in modern research design. The course counts as a general psychology elective for major or minor requirements.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Student is studying away this semester with a Partner Program.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: This course represents credit earned through a semester study abroad experience with an institution or program with which Texas Christian University has an official agreement to accept credit. The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30003, senior standing, and membership in the Honors Program. A supervised research experience and a thesis that is usually based on the subject matter studied in 30003. This course is offered only as a tutorial. Arrangements for this course must be made with an instructor the semester prior to enrollment. It is recommended that enrollment occur the fall semester of the senior year.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30003, senior standing, and membership in the Honors Program.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Fifteen semester hours in Psychology. This applied course extends learning beyond the classroom and provides development opportunities in leadership, diversity, counseling, etc. Students must obtain a volunteer or internship position (assistance is available through the instructor). Earned credit hours are based on the number of hours worked (up to 3 credit hours for 120 clock hours of work), attending class 1 hour per week, and completion of all assignments such as weekly journals and presentation handouts.
courses.prereqText: Fifteen semester hours in Psychology.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 40260. This experiential course provides advanced opportunities through volunteer or internship positions that may be paid or unpaid positions. Service environments provide experiential learning opportunities related to leadership, counseling, human resources or other arenas. Students obtain their own positions (assistance is provided by the instructor) and earned credit hours are based on the actual number of clock hours worked (e.g., 3 credit hours requires 150 clock hours of work), attending class 1 hour per week, and completion of all assignments.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 40260.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: 15 semester hours in Psychology, plus written permission of the professor and the psychology department. Projects in neuroscience research carried out under the direction of a faculty member. Because ongoing research projects differ from one semester to the next, students gain additional research skills each time they take the course. The course may be repeated twice (taken a maximum of three semesters in all.)
courses.prereqText: 15 semester hours in Psychology, plus written permission of the professor and the psychology department.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: 15 semester hours in Psychology, plus written permission of the professor and the psychology department. Projects in psychology of learning research carried out under the direction of a faculty member. Because ongoing research projects differ from one semester to the next, students gain additional research skills each time they take the course. The course maybe repeated twice (taken a maximum of three semesters in all.)
courses.prereqText: 15 semester hours in Psychology, plus written permission of the professor and the psychology department.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: 15 semester hours in Psychology, plus written permission of the professor and the psychology department. Projects in psychology of learning research carried out under the direction of a faculty member. Because ongoing research projects differ from one semester to the next, students gain additional research skills each time they take the course. The course maybe repeated twice (taken a maximum of three semesters in all.)
courses.prereqText: 15 semester hours in Psychology, plus written permission of the professor and the psychology department.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: 15 semester hours in Psychology, plus written permission of the professor and the psychology department. Projects in cognitive psychology carried out under the direction of a faculty member. Because ongoing research projects differ from one semester to the next, students gain additional research skills each time they take the course. The course may be repeated twice (taken a maximum of three semesters in all.)
courses.prereqText: 15 semester hours in Psychology, plus written permission of the professor and the psychology department.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Projects in developmental psychology carried out under the direction of a faculty member. Because ongoing research projects differ from one semester to the next, students gain additional research skills each time they take the course. The course may be repeated twice (taken a maximum of three semesters in all).

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Forensic psychology deals with the application of psychological knowledge or methods to tasks faced by the legal system. These tasks include: criminal investigation, assessing defendants for insanity or competency, assessing people for risk of violence, sexual offense, or other dangerous behaviors, trial consultation, child-custody evaluations, understanding interrogations, confessions, and eyewitness identification, and the selection and training of law enforcement officers.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213, 10514, or 10524 or approval of instructor. Credits cannot be given for both PSYC 40393 and 40403. Theories and techniques used in counseling in institutional, educational, and community settings; roles and functions of counselors; the relations of the counselor with clients and organizations.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213, 10514, or 10524 or approval of instructor. Credits cannot be given for both PSYC 40393 and 40403.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher. Counseling in institutional, educational, and community settings; roles and functions of counselors; the relations of the counselor in different settings with clients and organizations. Credit cannot be given for both PSYC 40393 and PSYC 40303.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503, Psychology or Neuroscience major, and junior standing and higher.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30323 or 30503 or 30453, or approval of instructor. Major periods of cognitive development including infancy, early childhood, middle childhood, and adolescence; development of cognitive skills such as reasoning, problem solving, memory, language, and perception; acquisition of applied cognitive skills such as arithmetic, reading, writing, and physics.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30323 or 30503 or 30453, or approval of instructor. Major periods of cognitive development including infancy, early childhood, middle childhood, and adolescence; development of cognitive skills such as reasoning, problem solving, memory, language, and perception; acquisition of applied cognitive skills such as arithmetic, reading, writing, and physics.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503, PSYC 30313, Psychology or Neuroscience or Child Development major, and junior standing and higher. Data and research methods related to the development of the human organism from its prenatal origins through old age..
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503, PSYC 30313, Psychology or Neuroscience or Child Development major, and junior standing and higher.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514 or 10524. This course will study child and adolescent development from a cross-cultural perspective. Topics include cross-cultural differences in historical conceptualizations of children, current government policies aimed at children and families, classroom learning, parenting (including the role of fathers) and differences in infants' temperaments.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524 and junior or senior standing. This course provides an overview of contemporary theory and research on gender and gender identity, and considers the societal, historical, intersectional, iintrapersonal, and interpersonal experiences of the members of each gender. The shared qualities of all genders and the progression toward equity and equality will also be discussed.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524 and junior or senior standing.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Psychology or Neuroscience major, junior standing and higher, PSYC 30463 or its equivalent, or approval of instructor. A topic seminar with an emphasis on developing an understanding of the interaction of the biological, genetic, psychological, and social factors that underlie the development of behavior.
courses.prereqText: Psychology or Neuroscience major, junior standing and higher, PSYC 30463 or its equivalent, or approval of instructor. A topic seminar with an emphasis on developing an understanding of the interaction of the biological, genetic, psychological, and social factors that underlie the development of behavior.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503. Characteristics of tests and measurement scales; survey of individual and group tests in psychology, education, and clinical settings.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524. This course will examine mental illness from a cross-cultural and creative perspective. Topics include cross-cultural differences in historical conceptualizations of mental illness, current government policies aimed at mental illness, examination of treatment and use of art (e.g., painting: Vincent Van Gogh, writing: Virginia Woolf) as a means of creativity in mental illness.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC10213. The course will look at the range of ethical decisions that are required of scientists. We will focus on identifying ethical dilemma throughout the history of scientific discovery. Case studies will include both moral exemplars and instances of scientific misconduct. These case studies will cut across scientific disciplines and include examples from biology, medical research, biotechnology, and psychology.
courses.prereqText: PSYC10213.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524. Health psychology is a field of study that examines the relationship between biological, psychological, and social factors that affect illness and wellness. This course is designed to give you a broad overview of the field of health psychology, including concepts, theory, research, and practice. Specific topics covered include stress and coping, health behaviors, chronic illnesses, and the health-care delivery system.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 30343 or PSYC 30353. An introduction to the science of attitudes and persuasion (i.e., attitude change). Topics include the origin, structure, function, and consequences of attitudes, as well as an overview of the major theories of persuasion.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30343 or PSYC 30353.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Psychology or Neuroscience major, junior standing and higher, PSYC30503. This course teaches students how to communicate psychological science effectively to both professional and public audiences.
