Students will learn to write and speak with clarity, accuracy, and engagement across a variety of formats, including journal articles, posters, TED-style talks, op-eds, podcasts, and social media. The course also explores the ethical and strategic use of AI tools for drafting, editing, and optimizing science communication. Emphasis will be placed on understanding your audience, telling compelling stories with data, and communicating complex ideas simply. A key focus of the course is iterative improvement: all major assignments will be submitted as drafts, receive feedback, and be revised for final grading.
courses.prereqText: Psychology or Neuroscience major, junior standing and higher, PSYC30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites:Written permission of the instructor of the course in which the student plans to serve. Students receive three credit hours for nine hours of duties per week, including mandatory weekly course meetings. Basic concepts of teaching and educational psychology. Basic concepts related to teaching and learning. Factors affecting teaching and learning. Pedagogical theories, techniques, and issues related to teaching psychology. Measurement and assessment in teaching and learning.
courses.prereqText: Written permission of the instructor of the course in which the student plans to serve.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prereq: Introduction to Psychology (PSYC 10213) or Principles of Behavior I (PSYC 105014) or Principles of Behavior II (PSYC 10524) and Research Methods in Psychology (PSYC 30503). This course examines intellectual and developmental disabilities across the lifespan, including characteristics, etiology, assessment, intervention, education, community services, family experiences, advocacy, and contemporary issues. Emphasis is placed on evaluating and synthesizing research and translating evidence into information relevant to professionals, individuals with developmental disabilities, and their families.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, or approval of instructor. Topics of current interest in psychology or society. This class carries 1-6 hours, but is usually offered for 3 hours credit.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213, or 10514, or 10524, or approval of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: PSYC 30503 and junior or senior standing in psychology. This course teaches students how to think critically about experimental psychology research topics, research methods and ethics, career pathways, and post-graduate opportunities in psychology. It is excellent preparation for graduate school in all areas of psychology and related disciplines.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503 and junior or senior standing in psychology.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 30503. Introduction to SPSS in application to research in the behavioral sciences, including use of SPSS functions for data analysis. Attention is also given to the use of univariate and multivariate methods of exploratory data analysis.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 30503.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: Permission from instructor. This course is designed to introduce students to using R, an open-source computing program. The course will focus on skills related to data visualization, data wrangling, transforming data, using functions, essential statistical functions, and a basic introduction to select machine learning/data driven methods. The course is split into three sections. Section 1: R fundamentals. Section 2: R for some statistical methods that you already know. Section 3: a first introduction to statistical learning/machine learning methods in R.
courses.prereqText: Permission from instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: permission of instructor. The current literature associated with the neurobiology of aging, modern research techniques and recent developments in neuroscience and aging research are discussed. This is a participation course in which advanced undergraduate and graduate students will present manuscripts, explain research hypotheses and methodologies and explain results. Open discussion of these papers will include faculty from Biology and Psychology. Topics presented will differ by semester. The course may be repeated three times (taken a maximum of four semesters in all.) (Crosslisted as BIOL/PSYC 50401.)
courses.prereqText: permission of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Graduate standing in psychology or permission of instructor. An in depth analysis of the neural and endocrine components of normal and abnormal behavior with emphasis on classic studies in the field.
courses.prereqText: Graduate standing in psychology or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Graduate or senior standing or permission of instructor. The fundamentals of functional neuroanatomy and neurophysiology with an emphasis on experimental and theoretical analysis of the basic brain behavior relationships. (Crosslisted as BIOL/PSYC 50463.)
courses.prereqText: Graduate or senior standing or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisites: 2.75 GPA in major, completion of either at least 20 credit hours in the department OR graduate status, and approval of department chair. Practical experience in the field of Psychology-related research that may involve work both at TCU and/or outside of TCU (but inside the state of Texas), including field work, internships, part-time jobs, and unpaid volunteer positions, all of which are to be centered around providing real-world training that would enhance the possibility of obtaining a career in a psychology-related research area. Must include a minimum of 260 work hours. This course may only be taken pass/no credit.
courses.prereqText: 2.75 GPA in major, completion of either at least 20 credit hours in the department OR graduate status, and approval of department chair.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524, and junior standing. Theory and principles of behavioral and biochemical methods of assaying drug action, with primary emphasis on the study of the effects of neuropharmacological agents or endogenous systems.
courses.prereqText: PSYC 10213 or 10514 or 10524, and junior standing.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Graduate standing in psychology or permission of instructor. The planning and design of behavioral research including the specification of research problems, development of appropriate designs, the use of appropriate analytic techniques and the interpretation of results. Primary attention is given to analysis of variance models as analytic techniques, but multivariate techniques such as regression and discriminant function models are also considered.
courses.prereqText: Graduate standing in psychology or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Junior standing. This course is designed to present an integrated and comprehensive overview of numerous issues in child development as well as treatments/solutions for those issues. This diverse array of developmental problems will be presented in a series of case-studies by professors from several departments as well as by community professionals who specialize in children's issues. This course is a requirement for the Child Development Minor as well as an elective course in Psychology. (Crosslisted as CHDV/PSYC 50533.)
courses.prereqText: Junior standing.

courses.subject: PSYC
courses.description: Prerequisite: Graduate standing in psychology, or permission of instructor. Selected theoretical principles important for understanding complex behavior, and their recent extensions and application to human social behavior, autonomic and psychosomatic function, etc.
courses.prereqText: Graduate standing in psychology, or permission of instructor. Selected theoretical principles important for understanding complex behavior, and their recent extensions and application to human social behavior, autonomic and psychosomatic function, etc.

courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: This course will explore the Triple Bottom Line of food production and distribution in an effort to measure organizational and societal successes based upon the economic, ecological, and social/cultural equation. The course will examine global food production, including the history of, the populations affected, as well as methodologies employed. The course will give overview of the current situation in global food production, distribution, and related challenges.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Methods of livestock identification, dehorning, castration, and controlling parasites; the planning and construction of fences, corrals, and buildings to facilitate the handling of livestock.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Soil formation and development; soil characteristics which affect productivity; soil erosion by wind and water; soil, water, and wildlife conservation and management practices; Soil and Water Conservation District and U.S.D.A. agency assistance; preparation of coordinated conservation plan.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Digestion and use of feeds for maintenance and production, selection of feeds for maintenance and production, selection of feeds based on composition and cost, ration formulation, feed processing and handling, dry lot feeding programs, supplemental feeding on pasture, possible limiting factors in feeding efficiency.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Prerequisites: Must successfully complete the entire fall semester of Ranch Management coursework with a semester GPA or 2.0 or greater, which includes RAMA 30102, 30403, 40103, 40303, 50503 and 50603. co-requisite courses - must remain in good standing with the Ranch Management program and be enrolled in the complete spring semester of Ranch Management coursework. These courses include RAMA 30703, 40112, 40313, 40903, 50213, and 50803. The capstone for the TCU Ranch Management Program requires students to apply knowledge and principles explored through all of their other coursework and learning activities. Students will design a complete ranch business management plan on an existing ranch land resource and inventory will be used to design and develop a business management plan for two separate enterprises: (1) cow/calf operation, and (2) a stock operation. The plan should incorporate principles that are sound on both an ecological basis and economical basis, while conserving and improving the ranch land resource.
courses.prereqText: Must successfully complete the entire fall semester of Ranch Management coursework with a semester GPA or 2.0 or greater, which includes RAMA 30102, 30403, 40103, 40303, 50503 and 50603. co-requisite courses - must remain in good standing with the Ranch Management program and be enrolled in the complete spring semester of Ranch Management coursework. These courses include RAMA 30703, 40112, 40313, 40903, 50213, and 50803.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Economics of beef production enterprises; selection by records and visual appraisal for economically important traits including reproduction, gainability, and carcass value; inheritance; systems of breeding; production programs; management practices.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Sheep breeds and crosses; selection for mutton and wool production; Angora goat selection; breeding; supplemental feeding; marketing of wool and mohair.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Anatomy and physiology of cattle, indications of health and disease, development of immunity, specific infectious and noninfectious diseases of cattle, control of internal and external parasites, toxicology, basic veterinary skills and equipment.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Reproduction in cattle including organs and functions, natural and artificial breeding management, calving management, examination of cows for pregnancy, evaluation of bulls for soundness and fertility, selection of horses for soundness, treatment for sickness and injury, horse breeding.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Reproduction in cattle including organs and functions, natural and artificial breeding management, calving management, examination of cows for pregnancy, evaluation of bulls for soundness and fertility, selection of horses for soundness, treatment for sickness and injury, horse breeding.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Basic records needed for management and income tax reports - records of income and expense, inventories, net worth statements, budgets, production records, sources of credit for ranch operations; business law as applied to the livestock producer, business organization, estate planning, labor relations, application of management principles to ranching.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Characteristics and management of introduced pasture plants; combinations for extended grazing, seedbed preparation and planting; weed control, fertilization, irrigation, grazing management and harvest for hay, silage and seed.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Business law as applied to the livestock producer, business organization, estate planning, labor relations, application of management principles to ranching.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Principles of plant growth and reproduction; economic characteristics and field identification of range plants; ecology of range plants and animals; management of rangeland for all its uses including setting and adjusting stocking rates, distribution of grazing, grazing methods and supporting practices; preparation of ranch management plan.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Basic records needed for management and income tax reports - records of income and expense, inventories, net worth statements, budgets, production records; term problem in which all records for a year's operation are recorded and financial statements are prepared; sources of credit for ranch operations.

courses.subject: RAMA
courses.description: Relation of production to marketing, trends in marketing and consumption, meat processing and distribution, U.S.D.A. activities, market outlets and procedures, futures, seasonal and cyclical influences on prices, selection of time and place to market, handling and transportation of livestock to improve weighing conditions and minimize losses, merchandising purebred livestock.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Transfer work with TCUCC-RT, HUM credit.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course introduces students to the vital role of religion in human experience by considering historical, comparative and methodological issues in the study of religion with reference to rituals, institutions, texts, figures, and beliefs in major world religions.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course introduces students to the vital role of religion in human experience by exploring literary, historical, cultural dimensions of religion texts, patterns of belief, and related ritual and ethical practices.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course introduces students to the vital role of religion in human experience. Through case studies, readings, lectures, and multimedia demonstrations, students will learn about the various relations between religion, culture, and society.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Topics may vary each time it is offered.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: An introduction to the grammar and vocabulary of the New Testament in the original Greek.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: An introduction to the writings in the New Testament with special attention to the content of the individual books, together with an understanding of the beginnings of the Christian faith seen through the study of the Gospels and the initial development of the Christian movement.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: What is the purpose of your education? How does it relate to creating a flourishing life, one filled with deep satisfaction, well-being, resilience, and accomplishment? What can we learn from the humanities and sciences about the varieties of human flourishing and its key ingredients, and how can you develop your own personal vision of that life? What skills and knowledge would you need to realize that vision? This course aims to assist you in finding your own answers to these questions so as to lay the foundation for flourishing during your undergraduate years, while also preparing you for a life of flourishing in personal, civic, and professional contexts. We will explore perspectives from both the humanities and sciences in ways that are directly relevant to university life, and we will engage in practices, such as mindfulness and meditation, which will help you develop the intellectual and emotional dispositions¿resilience, compassion, gratitude, and others¿that research shows are central to human flourishing.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: What's religion got to do with making moral decisions? In this introduction to religious ethics, students learn how to deepen their capacity to make moral choices by thinking about the interrelationship of modes of decision-making, social analyses and faith commitments. Then, using case studies, students explore how Muslims, Christians and Jews can provide moral leadership in civic discourse regarding ethical issues from pre-marital sex to economic justice.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This class examines the origins and impact of African civilization, focusing on the worlds of traditional religions, Islam and Christianity in Africa; colonialism, anti-colonial struggles, independence, and post-colonialism; African studies in Western Scholarship; and issues affecting modern Africa.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Building on RELI 20503, this class examines West African religious traditions, the 'involuntary diaspora' to the New World, as well as 'creole' religions and culture within the Caribbean. It concludes with an account of the rise of the African Independent Churches; the place of women in North African Islam; the presence of Rastafari in Ghana, and the continuing clash of traditional African and Western cultures.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: Religion major or permission of instructor. Must have completed introductory Religion course. This course considers the founders of three important religious traditions, both in their own right and as examples of what happens during the creation of a religious tradition. After considering the question what is religion? we turn to reports of the lives of Confucius, the Buddha, and Jesus Christ. We will inquire into how their cultural context shapes them, and how our cultural upbringing shapes the way we look at them.
courses.prereqText: Religion major or permission of instructor. Must have completed introductory Religion course.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: Religion major or permission of the instructor. Must have completed an introductory Religion course. This course will explore the varied ways in which different religions in various historical and cultural contexts address mortality and the question of life after death. By focusing on social constructions of death and post-mortem destiny in different religious traditions, students will encounter a range of beliefs, rituals and sacred narratives.
courses.prereqText: Religion major or permission of the instructor. Must have completed an introductory Religion course.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023 or 10033 or 10043. Through historical exploration, contemporary case studies, curated encounters, critical reflection, creative projects and individual research, students in this Sophomore Seminar will explore a variety of religions in contexts of conflict and cooperation in order to become informed students of religions and effective leaders in a religiously diverse world.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course examines two key events from the religious and cultural histories of China and India: the sixteenth-century Confucian debate over the legitimate successor to the Ming Dynasty's Wanli Emperor, and the division, or Partition, of the Indian subcontinent in 1947 into India and Pakistan. Both events represented a crisis in governance in which debate of the nation's future was informed by religious teachings. To investigate these two events, the course will use games from Reacting to the Past (RTTP), an interdisciplinary and highly engaging method of inquiry that requires students to study a variety of sources, debate, write, and work as a part of a group pursuing a set of shared goals.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: Religion major or permission of instructor. Must have completed an introductory Religion course. An introduction to theological reading, thinking, and writing through an exploration of major doctrines in Christian theology. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century developments, such as the rise of historical thinking and its impact on Christology, the rise of scientific thinking and its impact on the doctrine of creation, and the rise of postmodern thinking and its impact on Christian views of other religions will be emphasized. Class procedure will be seminar discussion of assigned readings.
courses.prereqText: Religion major or permission of instructor. Must have completed an introductory Religion course.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: Religion major or minor, or departmental permission. Introduces the role of the minister and outlines his/her responsibilities. Special emphasis on preaching, religious education (including youth work) and pastoral care.
courses.prereqText: Religion major or minor, or departmental permission.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: Religion major or permission of instructor. Must have completed introductory Religion course. This course explores the present and potential role of novels, religious theory and literary criticism in understanding religion's nature and function. The seminar's focus draws from one of the following three topics: World Faiths, World Fictions, Pilgrimage, and Nonwestern Christianity.
courses.prereqText: Religion major or permission of instructor. Must have completed introductory Religion course.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course represents credit earned through a semester study abroad experience with an institution or program with which Texas Christian University has an official agreement to accept credit. The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Creative dialogue between religion and other disciplines of learning, or aspects of culture.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: A careful look at early Christian gospels, including Thomas, and at how scholars construct a historical Jesus from them.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: The developing origins of Christianity, with particular emphasis on Paul and his influence.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Study of the biblical books of Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Job within their own socio-historic contexts as a basis for investigating some of the fundamental questions of human religious experience, including the function of worship, the relationship of reason and faith, the problem of evil, and the bases of ethical behavior.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10033, or permission of the instructor. The course explores the rich and diverse world of the ancient Jewish texts discovered in the caves near Khirbet Qumran. Known also as the Dead Sea scrolls, these texts shed light on almost every aspect of what came to be know as the Second Temple period. Yet, they proved to be particularly important for understanding the complex religious and social matrix out of which emerged nascent Christianity and Rabbinic Judaism. The course takes a closer look at this matrix by means of reading a variety of texts from Qumran.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10033, or permission of the instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043, or permission of instructor. Explores distinctive characteristics of biblical narrative and investigates why readers produce different interpretations of biblical stories. It asks how social structures and value systems, ancient and modern, affect texts and interpreters.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043 or permission of the instructor. Women were clearly active and important participants in early Christianity, and yet we know relatively little about the female disciples, prophets, apostles, and deacons. This course will ask what information the historical record holds and how it can be mined to reconstruct who the women of early Christianity were, what was important to them, what they did, and the differences they made.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043 or permission of the instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023 or 10033 or 10043, or permission of instructor. In this course, we will study Biblical prophets and prophetic texts, with attention to their historical and literary contexts, as well as their religious and social functions. We will also consider the rhetorical and poetic dimensions of biblical prophecy, in order to reflect on both the positive and negative impact of religiously charged communication.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023 or 10033 or 10043, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course introduces students to the genocide of the Jewish people during World War II known as the Holocaust or Shoah. It focuses primarily on three aspects of the Holocaust. First, it explores the history of what has been called ¿the oldest hatred¿¿antisemitism¿that made the Holocaust possible. Second, it introduces students to the stories of the victims, perpetrators,collaborators, bystanders, and¿the precious few¿rescuers. Third, it invites students to consider a variety of theological responses to the Holocaust, by Jews and Christians.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course considers the historical mystical tradition within Christianity. Throughout the history of Christian thought individuals have appealed to mysticism to finding God. Some have used mysticism for finding God even in the midst of distress and suffering. We will consider topics such as Reading Scripture, Contemplation, the Spiritual Practices including prayer and fasting.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023 or 10033 or 10043 (one Understanding Religion introductory course). This course will explore a wide range of core spiritual practices that have shaped Christian individuals and communities across time.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023 or 10033 or 10043 (one Understanding Religion introductory course).

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: An introduction (beginning with the Bible) to major perspectives, with particular focus on developments since the Reformation. The student will argue a contemporary issue from a historical perspective.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: A study of developments in Christian thought, practice, and institutions from the beginnings of the church through the 15th century.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: A study of developments in Western Christianity from the 16th century Reformation to the 20th century, with attention to issues of theology, institutions, and practices. Does not include religion in America.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Explores the relationship between race and religion, and surveys African-American religious history in the United States, from the religious commitments of enslaved Africans to contemporary American black people's faiths.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course explores the history, development, and characteristics of evangelicalism in the United States. It will proceed both chronologically and topically, focusing more heavily on the post World War II period and contemporary American culture. It will consider a diverse range of personalities, communities, and subjects ranging from Billy Graham and presidential politics to "True Love Waits" and evangelical romance novels.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Roman Catholicism in the modern period with particular attention given to the Second Vatican Council and its intellectual and institutional implications. There will be some emphasis on American Catholicism.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043 or permission of instructor. Applying the 'influencer' concept to the study of Asian religions, this course explores how religion, like social media, provides a potent platform for religious women to influence how cultures think about gender norms and opportunities for women's greater freedom. It examines women's authority in Asian religions through multiple perspectives with a focus on 'charisma' and 'spiritual genius.' Furthermore, it stresses ethnographic approaches that elevate women's roles and other cultural variables to understand how charisma motivates women's experiences of spiritual genius, and orients their relationship to power and leadership, tradition and innovation, religion and modernity in Asian cultures.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: The categories sect and cult in religion studies, with illustrations from existing groups, both within and outside the Christian tradition, e.g., Hasidic Judaism, Jehovah's Witnesses, Christian Science, Baha'i, the Amish, and Mormonism.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course will investigate the variety of religious life found among U.S. Latina/os, looking beyond misconceptions, generalizations and stereotypes.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course helps students think about religion by centering women's experiences and critical ideas about theology and ethics. Students will be introduced to Womanist religious thought and race-class-gender analytical approaches to examining religious life and society.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course is an advanced exploration of how digital technology is affecting the moral and religious sensibilities of contemporary culture, with a particular focus on how this technology is changing assumptions about God, the soul and morality.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course examines the role of religion and law in the formation of identity by exploring the notion that identity, including race, is a social construct by examining how various immigrant groups from around the world were and are shaped by religion and the American legal process. In particular, we will consider Latinos/as in the U.S. as an example of how law and religion shape a cultural group's identity as well as how law and religion impact cultural and global self-understanding.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: An exploration of the diverse strands of the Hindu religious tradition (ritual, philosophical, devotional) from the Vedic period to the modern day.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Examines the development of Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism. The course will explore the religious worldviews of these East Asian traditions in historical and cultural context, as well as issues relating to the comparative study of religions.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: The development of Buddhism in India, Southeast Asia, Tibet, China, Japan, and North America. Material will range from the Buddha's life to contemporary forms of Buddhism in America.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: The Islamic religious tradition from 7th century Arabia to current resurgence, including social, theological, and mystical dimensions. Topics include Muslim views of Allah, revelation the Qur'an, and the Prophet Muhammad. Islam's encounter with "modernity" will also be addressed.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Explores the worldviews, beliefs and practices of African Traditional Religions. Also examines the impact of Christianity and Islam on African Traditional Religions since the colonial period.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: The course is an introduction to many of the historical forms and manifestations of Judaism. The goal of this course is to examine Judaism conceptually, considering topics such as literature, politics, art, history and ritual, and to provide the student with a conceptual basis that will facilitate the comparison of Judaism with other world religions.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023, or permission of the Instructor. This course comprises an intellectual and imaginative journey into the fascinating world of Hindu and Buddhist goddess traditions in South Asian and Western culture contexts. It utilizes various types of primary resources to understand the nature, role, and purpose of South Asian goddess traditions within local and global landscapes, while foregrounding ethnographic and life history materials, to make meaningful sense of lived religion in the contemporary world.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023, or permission of the Instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: The world's religions espouse ethical values that inform their understanding of issues such as the value of human life, labor, and products. These religions have also had complicated and uneasy relationships with money and commerce, especially the ethics of trading and the accumulation of wealth. This course will explore the issues of money, wealth, and value through the lens of five religious traditions: Christianity,Hinduism, Buddhism, Islam, and Jainism.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This survey course will introduce students to historical developments, key figures and institutions within the history of Catholic Christianity from the High Middle Ages (ca. 1250) to the present. The course will begin by examining the roots of high medieval Catholic expansion into East Asia and its subsequent expansion into other continents during the Late Middle Ages. It will then examine the development of Catholicism in those geographic areas outside the USA, Western Europe, Australia and Russia. This course is an opportunity for students to take a pilgrimage into Catholic Christian identity across time and across the globe, primarily in those areas colonized by European kingdoms and nations. Topics such as colonialism, missions, enslavement, religious movements, enculteration, spiritual practices, indigenous clergy and local religious life will be examined in their historical context. The overall aim of the course is to deepen students' capacities for historical reflection on Catholic culture, beliefs, practices and institutions across the globe. Participants, whatever their religious identity (or lack thereof), will learn more of what it has meant historically to think, pray and live as Catholic Christians in the Majority World so that they can apply these insights to their own work in today's pluralistic context.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course surveys the role of religion in various social, cultural and political movements in Latin America beginning in the 18th century through present day. Primary and secondary documentary sources, spiritual autobiographies, multimedia productions, and news media help students consider how religion intersects with politics, economy, race, gender, and power throughout Latin American's history.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: PHIL 10003 or any religion course. This course is centrally concerned with issues relating to the rationality and justification of religious convictions. There is also an interest in the coherence of religious concepts. Various philosophical models for understanding and evaluating religious convictions and practices are examined and applied.
courses.prereqText: PHIL 10003 or any religion course.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: 3 semester hours of Religion or Philosophy. An exploration of ideas of God as they have developed in Western theology and philosophy since the 17th century. The relation between these ideas and current models for thinking about God will be stressed.
courses.prereqText: 3 semester hours of Religion or Philosophy.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the major trends, developments, and issues in modern Islamic thought and the global Muslim world. This course begins in the nineteenth century with the transformations caused by the rise of European power, European colonialism, modern science and technology, the printing press, mass education, and the nation state. Muslims around the world responded to these transformations through several strategies including modernism, fundamentalism, secularism, and neo-traditionalism. We will examine these and other trends, as well as Muslim perspectives on a range of pressing contemporary global issues such as politics, violence, gender, economics, science, technology, and the environment. The course concludes with a look at possible futures of the global Muslim world.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: ANTH 20623, RELI 10023 or RELI 10043 or consent of the instructor. Anthropological findings in the comparative study of religion and culture across a broad range of societies. Studies of sacred experience, myth, ritual, magic, witchcraft, religious language, gender and religion, healing, and relationships between social and religious change.
courses.prereqText: ANTH 20623, RELI 10023 or RELI 10043 or consent of the instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: SOCI 20213, or SOCI 20223 or permission of instructor. An introduction to understanding the role of religion in society and to sociological methods for the study of religion. The course will introduce theories and research pertaining to types of religious experience, conversion and commitment, denominationalism, secularization and fundamentalism. Class, gender, race and ethnicity will also be addressed as they influence religion in society. (Offered as RELI or SOCI credit.)
courses.prereqText: SOCI 20213, or SOCI 20223 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: Successful completion of either RELI 10023, 10033, or 10043, or consent of instructor. This course explores Native American perspectives on religion (spirituality) and contemporary issues, and compares them with Western-Christian perspectives. Students will read, discuss, and evaluate ideas put forth by important Native American authors, compare traditional Native American ways of knowing (epistemology) with Western-Christian ways, identify and critique stereotypes related to Native American perspectives, and apply these ideas to contemporary issues. Topics will vary by semester. Additionally, students will be in dialog with Native American community leaders on these topics.
courses.prereqText: Successful completion of either RELI 10023, 10033, or 10043, or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: 3 hours of Religion and any 6 hours from among Biology, Chemistry, Environmental Science, Geology, Physics, and Psychology. An exploration of the ways of knowing utilized in religion (particularly the Judeo-Christian heritage) and in science, and how these ways of knowing relate.
courses.prereqText: of Religion and any 6 hours from among Biology, Chemistry, Environmental Science, Geology, Physics, and Psychology.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043, or permission of instructor. An examination of concepts of mysticism and mystical experience. Examples will be drawn from Christian, Hindu, and Buddhist sources.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course explores religion and art as sources of existential meaning. Looking at the convergence of spirituality and creativity in works from Kandinsky to Basquiat and in writings from Kierkegaard to W.E.B. Du Bois, this class examines how art and religion hold out the promise of authenticity, meaning, and purpose.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course considers the many images of the god Krishna in the literary and religious imagination of the Indian people. After introducing some background of Hindu thought and practice, we shall look at how Krishna appears in different versions and interpretations of the great Indian epic, the Mahabharata, including the famous portion call the Bhagavad Gita. We then examine how Krishna appears in later devotional literature and poetry in the classical Sanskrit tradition, and finally Krishna in popular and regional understandings up to the present day. Credit cannot be granted for both RELI 30773 and RELI 30753.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: Either one RELI or one ANTH course, or permission of instructor. This course studies the cultures of Syria-Palestine and TransJordan from approximately 1550-332 BCE by identifying and interpreting the relevant archaeological data and anthropological findings. It will explore various aspects of these ancient cultures, including the region's economic, political, environmental, and social relations, as well as its religious expressions and ethnic identities. Additionally, students will consider the significance of archaeological material and anthropological models for reconstructing and interpreting these cultures and for understanding the Hebrew Bible as a cultural and historical document.
courses.prereqText: Either one RELI or one ANTH course, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course explores key elements of Native religious traditions through engagement with Indigenous feminisms and Two-Spirit/Queer Indigenous theories. The course traces the connections between Native religions, genders, and sexualities by exploring foundational theories in Native feminist and Indigenous queer writings.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Explores the ethical challenge of increased competition for world resources. Examines how changing religious understandings of stewardship, fairness and rights shape moral choice in issues like distribution of goods, care of nature and population shifts.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023, or permission of the instructor. This course examines the history, sacred texts, personalities, and practices of Hindu and Buddhist mysticisms in South Asia. It also investigates the lives of Buddhist and Hindu women mystical practitioners in text and practice and explores the extents to which Indian mystical systems enable women to empower themselves in Indic society.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023, or permission of the instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023, or 10033, or 10043, or permission of the instructor. This course will explore the role of religion, religious ethics and values in society and news media. Students will study methods of covering religion, investigate the importance of religion in the news media, and raise questions about the content of religious news stories.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023, or 10033, or 10043, or permission of the instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course explores the religious themes found within black literature for the purpose of developing new interdisciplinary methods and validating the use of black literary analysis for the study of black religion. The course introduces interdisciplinary methods and approaches to religious inquiry about the nature and meaning of God, religious experiences, community, and culture. Particular attention will be given to the black woman's literary tradition.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Over the past fifty years many creative writers and movie makers have attempted portraits of Jesus and Christ-figures in fiction and film. This course will identify the christological themes in these portraits and examine their importance for the development of contemporary Christian theology.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course investigates selected Christian thinkers and doctrinal themes as revealed in various classic and contemporary novels.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: In this course we will investigate and analyze discourses put forward by Latinas within the religious/theological field and how they fit the larger picture of Latina Feminisms in the United States.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Explores the experiences of women in American religion with attention to the interplay between women's religious identities and their roles in the work force, families, and racial, ethnic and/or minority groups. Readings will be drawn from historical, sociological and theological works.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Case studies of religiously inspired violence against those considered other or outside specific religious groups, examined through the lens of classic and contemporary religious theory. Special attention to the Middle East and Asia.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Explores the growth and spread of Islam in America. Introduces students to different Islamic groups and how they relate to each other. Discusses Muslims' responses to different challenges and criticism of Islam and Muslims by the media. Explains the roles of African Americans and women in Islamic institutions in America.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043, or permission of instructor. This interdisciplinary course investigates the spread as well as emergence of Rastafari religion, culture, and politics in Jamaica and other parts of the African diaspora.
courses.prereqText: RELI 10023, 10033, 10043, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Directed Study in Religion.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: This course treats the major figures, controversies and theological developments on the Christian idea of salvation as it is understood across the globe. The course will guide students chronologically from the earliest days of the religion to the present-day ecumenical movement. The course focuses on pivotal moments and figures in the Christian tradition and their contributions to the larger question: What must humans do to attain salvation?

(3-6 semester hours)
courses.prereqText: RELI 10033 or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: At least six hours in Religion, or permission of instructor. Critical analysis of gender relationships in biblical literature, society, and religion, with attention to the relevance of biblical values to today's society.
courses.prereqText: At least six hours in Religion, or permission of instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisites: RELI 10023, or 10033 or 10043. This course looks at religion and art as two significant modes of meaning making within the context of the postmodern challenge to systems of ultimate value.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: A survey of the major events and developments in religion in the United States, taking into account the development of institutions and thought patterns in terms of their interaction with the American context.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: Senior standing and 12 hours in Religion. Capstone seminar exploring selected issues, themes, or methods in the academic study of religion.
courses.prereqText: Senior standing and 12 hours in Religion.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: A critical study of ethical inquiry in a pluralistic world by focusing on proposals for a global ethic, scholarship on interreligious dialogue and research in comparative religious ethics. Students write proposals for promoting moral consensus on an international issue.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: A seminar dealing with a significant topic such as religion in art, church history, or contemporary issues, conducted in appropriate locations in this country or abroad. Specific topic will be defined as course is scheduled. Admission to course through application by announced deadline. (1-6 semester hours)

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Prerequisite: 3 semester hours of Religion, or permission of the instructor. This course looks at the theological significance of gender, and race in environmental ethics and helps students understand the historical descriptions of the role of nature in Scripture and Christian history, theological formulations from an ecological perspective, ethical grounding for the Christian practice of eco-justice and earthkeeping.
courses.prereqText: 3 semester hours of Religion, or permission of the instructor.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: The relationships between religious institutions and civil authority in America. While providing a historic context for the study, the course is primarily issue-oriented, dealing with such topics as prayer and Bible reading in public schools, state aid to parochial schools, conscientious objection to military service, Sunday closing laws, and taxation of churches.

courses.subject: RELI
courses.description: Assigned special problems in religion. (1-3 semester hours)

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: This course explores the interplay between science, engineering, technology and health care. Students will leave the course with a better understanding of the diseases that plague the American population, the treatment/intervention strategies, and some of the economic and ethic issues associated with the choice. This working knowledge offered is intended to make students better health consumers and self-advocates.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: General Transfer Credit

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisite: A senior high school course in STEM field and Recipient of STEM Scholarship. This course will serve as the first introduction to a college course. In this course, we will critically examine the chemical and physical properties of water, the role water plays in shaping the world, and how water is essential for life. As a class, we will analyze various ways to think about water, including as drinking water, a sanitation mechanism, and an economic resource. The ultimate goal of this class is to help you develop a deeper understanding of water while developing your critical thinking, presentation skills and writing skills.
courses.prereqText: A senior high school course in STEM field and Recipient of STEM Scholarship.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisite: Sophomore standing. This study abroad course is for students who are driven with an entrepreneurial spirit and have a passion for technological innovation. This course consists of lecture, invited speakers, case studies, and field trips.
courses.prereqText: Sophomore standing.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: This is a one-hour exploratory course for students in the College of Science & Engineering, particularly those on the pre health track, who are seeking career information related to academic and occupational interest patterns outside of the pre health track with STEM degrees. Students will be provided career development tools and resources such as career assessments, information on career options for their degree both traditional and non-traditional. Students will also have the opportunity to participate in career planning as it pertains to their strengths, skills, and interests.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Two hours of lecture and two hours of laboratory. Whiskey embodies multiple sciences and engineering. Whiskey has played a significant role in history including that of the United States. The course conveys elementary science concepts from the disciplines of chemistry, plant biology, genetics, neuroscience and engineering along with the historical underpinnings of these concepts as well as the impact that whiskey has had on US history since the colonial era up to and including multinational corporations. Laboratory experiments are linked intimately to lecture content.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Whisky serves as a useful lens for looking at science, history, culture and their interdependence. The course meets weekly for 2.5h in the spring semester to perform labs, discuss historical and cultural readings, and practice cultural activities. During the term, the group travels to an environment (ie Scotland, Ireland, Japan) for approximately two weeks for immersion in the course material to allow synthesis.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: The advancements of science and technology have accelerated over the past century, leading to corresponding societal advances and impacts on different communities. While much of the public thinks these advances are natural, many are, in fact, the result of sustained commitment by the nation to support science and technology through a deliberate set of policies. Federal policies affect science and technology on small and large scales, from undergraduate training grants to National Laboratories to State Department. Issues such as global climate change, energy sustainability, terrorism, nuclear proliferation, human genomics, and exponentially evolving technologies are among the most challenging and complex facing contemporary society and their impacts on local and native communities. This course will highlight the important role of national science policy in how science is used to affect large scale national and international policy decisions and how these decisions have or may impact minority and disadvantaged communities.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisites: SCIE 10503 and Recipient of STEM Scholarship from TCU. The course aims to introduce students to the different research opportunities, institutes, and initiatives in the College of Science and Engineering at TCU and beyond. Research in the areas of Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Computer Sciences, Psychology and Engineering will be highlighted. Students attend weekly meeting to discuss research opportunities in the College of Science and Engineering. Students will also learn about summer research opportunities outside of TCU.
courses.prereqText: SCIE 10503 and Recipient of STEM Scholarship from TCU.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: This course introduces new pre-health students to the concepts of readiness and expectations as a TCU pre-health student. Students will learn about resources available from the Pre-health Professions Institute, activities and life experiences that will best prepare them for their undergraduate pre-health career, and how to foster a community of support with their peers. Pass/No Credit grade basis only.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: This course will introduce students to critical global health concepts including the determinants of health, the measurements of health status, the importance of culture to health, the global burden of disease, key risk factors for different health conditions, demographic and epidemiological transitions, and the organization and functions of health systems.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: This course explores the relation between healthcare and visual culture of the human body. Drawing on a variety of academic disciplines and social productions, students will reflect on perceptions of the body and health in the historical and contemporary western, American medical context. Students will engage¿ and to a limited extent create¿visual media in conjunction with their course readings. This course is suited for those preparing for roles as healthcare professionals with the goal of developing empathetic ways of relating to others, namely patients suffering illness and in pain.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Topics of current interest. May be repeated for credit when the topic changes. (1-3 credit hours.)

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisites: ENGL 20803 or 20833. This study abroad course examines the rise of both science and technology in western civilization and how they have shaped history, with particular focus on developments in England. Includes visits to sites in London, Greenwich, Cambridge, and Oxford.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisite: 54 or more cumulative hours. Two hours of lecture and two hours laboratory. Whiskey embodies multiple sciences and engineering. Whiskey has played a significant role in history including that of the United States. The course conveys elementary science concepts from the disciplines of chemistry, plant biology, genetics, neuroscience and engineering along with the historical underpinnings of these concepts as well as the impact that whiskey has had on US history since the colonial era up to and including multinational corporations. Laboratory experiments are linked intimately to lecture content. Credit will not be granted for both SCIE 20303 and SCIE 30303.
courses.prereqText: 54 or more cumulative hours.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisites: Senior Standing. This capstone seminar course for the Cultural Awareness in Healthcare (CAH) minor will guide students through a process of synthesis and reflection based on each student¿s unique selection of coursework for the minor. Students will apply their knowledge and skills to the problem of healthcare disparities (locally, regionally, and globally), demonstrate their ability to engage in collective dialogue, and learn to articulate their cultural competence for their future career in healthcare or related field. This course is intended for all students who have completed a minimum of 15 hours of the CAH minor coursework and are in the final semester(s) of their undergraduate degree plan.
courses.prereqText: Senior Standing. This capstone seminar course for the Cultural Awareness in Healthcare (CAH) minor will guide students through a process of synthesis and reflection based on each student¿s unique selection of coursework for the minor.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisite: Sophomore standing. This course explores the relation between religion and healthcare in the American medical context. We will trace the historic interplay between religious practice and fostering human health in the West, with emphasis on the prominence of Christianity, the development of secularism, and religious plurality that marks contemporary healthcare. This course is suited for those preparing for roles as healthcare professionals, with the goal of fostering cultural competence.
courses.prereqText: Sophomore standing.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisites: BIOL 30603 and CHEM 30123. This course will introduce students to the concept of professionalism within a healthcare context and the core competencies that future healthcare providers should possess. Students will reflect on how their work, activities and life experiences have prepared them for a career in healthcare. Additionally, students will develop written and verbal communication skills applicable to health professions and the professional school application process.
courses.prereqText: BIOL 30603 and CHEM 30123.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisites: Written permission of the instructor of the course in which the student plans to serve. Students serve as teaching assistants for professional development courses designed for Pre-Health students. Students receive one credit hour for every three hours of course-related duties per week including course staff meetings, consultations with students, assisting with grading and other duties as assigned.
courses.prereqText: Written permission of the instructor of the course in which the student plans to serve.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisites: BIOL 10503 and 10513. Students will examine the dietary requirements of both animals and livestock and be exposed to basic anatomy, physiology and biochemistry of the gastrointestinal system, nutrient procurement and use, feed additives, growth stimulants, metabolic disease and diet therapy.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: This course represents credit earned through a semester study abroad experience with an institution or program with which Texas Christian University has an official agreement to accept credit. The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisites: Completion of SCIE 20907, a minimum of 48 credit hours, and with instructor's approval. This seminar explores the intersection of storytelling and healthcare, emphasizing the importance of narrative competence/humility in medical practice. In this seminar, students will engage with literature, film, and personal narratives to develop a deeper understanding of patients' experiences and the role of empathy and compassion in healthcare. Through critical analysis and reflective writing, students will learn to appreciate the complexities of illness, enhance their listening skills, and cultivate the ability to acknowledge, interpret, and respond to patients' stories. This seminar is suited for pre-health students-ideally on the pre-medical and pre-PA track-who are seeking to integrate compassionate, patient-centered care into their future clinical practice
courses.prereqText: Completion of SCIE 20907, a minimum of 48 credit hours, and with instructor's approval.

courses.subject: SCIE
courses.description: Prerequisites Students must be pursuing the cultural awareness and healthcare minor and have completed 60 hours of coursework. This course is available to students pursuing the Cultural Awareness in Healthcare minor. Research and other scholarly experiences for advanced students. Three clock hours per week of research are required for each semester hour of credit, for up to three semester hours credit in any given semester. This course can be repeated or taken in combination with SCIE 40633 for maximum of six hours of credit between the two courses.

courses.description: This course explores differing patterns of human relationships; the course further applies sociological concepts so as to enrich the understanding of human behavior.

courses.subject: SOCI
courses.description: This course presents information about a range of social problems (poverty, racism, sexual discrimination, crime, etc.) with emphasis on the relationship between the individual and the larger context within which the problems exist. Additionally, fundamental societal institutions and theoretical issues will be explored.

courses.subject: SOCI

The site and specific content will be identified on the official transcript. Courses appearing on a student's official transcript have been included in the student's grade point average.
